slides.title: Rita's week at the clinic
text: Last spring, Rita spent a week at a vet clinic in Braga as part of a school project. She thought she would spend the days cuddling puppies. She was wrong.

On Monday she cleaned cages and answered the phone. On Tuesday she watched a vet stitch up a cat after an operation, and she nearly fainted. By Thursday she was helping to weigh dogs and enter the data on the computer.

"The hardest part wasn't the blood," she says. "It was talking to owners when their pet was really ill." Rita still wants to be a vet, but now she knows the job needs patience and good people skills, not just a love of animals.

slides.title: A lucky mess
text: In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming was studying bacteria in his laboratory in London. He wasn't famous for being tidy. Before going on holiday, he left some dishes of bacteria on his bench.

When he came back, he noticed something strange. A mould had grown on one of the dishes, and around it the bacteria had died. Fleming realised the mould was producing a substance that killed germs. He called it penicillin.
It took other scientists more than ten years to turn it into a medicine that hospitals could use. Since then, antibiotics like penicillin have saved millions of lives. Not bad for a messy desk.

text: Tiago used to buy a new T-shirt almost every weekend. They were cheap, so why not? Then his Geography teacher showed the class how much water it takes to grow the cotton for just one shirt. Tiago started counting the shirts in his wardrobe. He had forty-one.
Most fast fashion is made in factories far away, often by workers who earn very little. The clothes are designed to be worn a few times and then replaced.

slides.title: Two days at the supermarket door
text: Twice a year, the Banco Alimentar Contra a Fome collects food in supermarkets all over Portugal. Last December, Beatriz, 15, signed up with three friends from her class.

Their job was simple: stand at the door, hand out plastic bags and explain the campaign. "At first I was really shy," she admits. "Some people walked past without looking at us. But an old man came back with a bag full of rice and milk and said, 'I was helped once. Now it's my turn.'"
By Sunday evening, their supermarket had collected more than a tonne of food. "My feet hurt," Beatriz says, "but I'm going again in May."

slides.title: One street, many languages
text: Amira lives in Mouraria, one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Lisbon. Her parents came from Bangladesh twelve years ago and run a small grocery shop near Martim Moniz.

"On my way to school I hear Bengali, Nepali, Chinese, Portuguese and Cabo Verdean Creole, all before eight o'clock," she says. At home she speaks Bengali; with her friends she speaks Portuguese; online she games in English.

Not everything is easy. Some people still ask her where she is "really" from. "I was born at Santa Maria Hospital," she laughs. "I'm from here." In June she goes to the Santo António parties like everyone else, and she always eats more sardines than her friends.

slides.title: Eight countries, one language
text: Last March, Duarte's class from Viseu went on an Erasmus+ exchange to a school in Finland. There were students from eight countries, and nobody spoke Finnish except the hosts.
"I thought my English wasn't good enough," Duarte says. "But then I realised the Italians and the Czechs were making mistakes too, and nobody cared. We just wanted to understand each other."

The hardest person to understand? A teacher from Scotland. "He spoke so fast! The Finnish kids spoke more slowly and clearly than him." By the end of the week, the group had a chat with forty messages a minute, all in a kind of English that worked perfectly for them.

slides.title: Diwali: the festival of lights
text: Diwali is one of the most important festivals in India. It is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, usually in October or November, and it lasts about five days.

Before Diwali, families clean their homes and buy new clothes. At night they light small clay lamps called diyas and put them in windows and doorways. The lights represent the victory of light over darkness and good over evil.

There are fireworks, sweets and big family meals. Diwali is also celebrated in the UK: the city of Leicester holds one of the biggest Diwali celebrations outside India, with thousands of people in the streets.

slides.title: The girl who wouldn't stay quiet
text: Malala Yousafzai grew up in the Swat Valley in Pakistan. When she was eleven, an armed group took control of the area and began closing girls' schools. Malala started writing a blog about her life for the BBC, using a false name.
In 2012, when she was fifteen, a gunman stopped her school bus and shot her in the head. She survived after treatment in Birmingham, England, and continued her campaign.
In 2014, at seventeen, she won the Nobel Peace Prize, the youngest person ever to receive it. "One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world," she said at the United Nations.

slides.title: True or false?
slides.instruction: Read the text again. Correct the false sentences.

items.q: Malala is from Afghanistan.
items.fix: She is from Pakistan.

items.q: She wrote a blog under her real name.
items.fix: She used a false name.

items.q: She was attacked on her way to or from school.
She received treatment in England.
She won the Nobel Peace Prize at twenty-one.
items.fix: She won it at seventeen.

slides.title: Making opposites
slides.note: There's no perfect rule for **un-** and **in-**: check a dictionary and learn the word with its prefix.

slides.title: Add a prefix
slides.instruction: Complete with the opposite of the word in brackets.

items.q: It's ___ (fair) that girls can't go to school there.
Laughing at someone's accent is really ___ (respectful).
Some people are ___ (tolerant) of other religions.
Leaving rubbish on the beach is ___ (responsible).
Don't be so ___ (patient)! The bus will come.
Selling fake brands is ___ (legal) in Portugal.

items.en: **I totally agree.** Everyone should learn about other cultures.
**That's a good point, but** fair trade products are more expensive.
**I see what you mean, but I'm not sure** that one person can change much.
**I'm afraid I disagree.** Jokes about accents can really hurt.
**It depends.** Some jokes are fine, others aren't.

slides.title: Respond politely
slides.instruction: Choose the most polite and natural reply.

items.q: "Racist jokes are just jokes."
options: I'm afraid I disagree. They hurt people.
items.a: I'm afraid I disagree. They hurt people.

items.q: "We should all buy fair trade chocolate."
options: That's a good point, but it's expensive.
items.a: That's a good point, but it's expensive.

items.q: "Learning about other religions is useful."
"Social media makes people less tolerant."

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: Have you ever seen someone treated unfairly? What did you do?
Do you think of yourself as a global citizen? Why?
Would you pay more for fair trade products?
Where does prejudice come from, in your opinion?
What would you ask Malala if you met her?

slides.title: Remember
points: Disagree politely: **I see what you mean, but...**

decks.title: Stereotypes
decks.subtitle: Do all Portuguese people eat bacalhau every day?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: explain what a **stereotype** is and why it can be harmful
tell the difference between a **fact** and an **opinion**
use language to **avoid generalising**
check information before you believe or **share** it

cards.heading: Stereotype
cards.text: A simple, fixed idea about a whole group of people.

cards.heading: Prejudice
cards.text: A negative feeling about someone because of their group.
cards.example: not trusting someone for their accent

cards.heading: Discrimination
cards.text: Treating someone worse because of that prejudice.
cards.example: not giving someone a job for their name

slides.title: How others see us, how we see them
Not what I expected
text: When Leonor moved to Manchester with her family, she had a list of things she "knew" about the English. They were cold and quiet, they ate boiled vegetables and they never left the house without an umbrella.

On her first day at school, a girl called Priya hugged her and asked if she wanted to sit together. Her neighbours invited them for a curry. And nobody at school owned an umbrella: they just pulled up their hoods.

The English had some ideas about her too. "Do you speak Spanish at home?" a boy asked. "And do you know Ronaldo?" Leonor laughed. "No and no. But I know where to find the best pastéis de nata in Manchester."

slides.title: True or false?
slides.instruction: Read the text again. Correct the false sentences.

items.q: Leonor had fixed ideas about the English before she moved.
Priya was unfriendly on Leonor's first day.
items.fix: Priya hugged her and asked her to sit together.

items.q: Her neighbours invited them for a roast dinner.
items.fix: They invited them for a curry.

items.q: Her classmates used hoods instead of umbrellas.
A boy thought Portuguese people speak Spanish.

slides.title: Fact or opinion?
slides.text: A **fact** can be checked and proved. An **opinion** is what someone thinks or feels. Words like **best**, **worst**, **beautiful** and **boring** often signal opinions.
examples: Fact: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal.
Opinion: Lisbon is the most beautiful city in Europe.
Fact: The UK uses the pound. Opinion: British food is boring.

slides.title: Fact or opinion?
slides.instruction: Decide if each sentence is a fact or an opinion.

items.q: Portuguese is spoken on four continents.
English is easier than French.
Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.
Fado is the saddest music in the world.
The Tagus flows into the Atlantic Ocean.
Teenagers spend too much time online.

slides.title: How to avoid generalising
rows: **There's no evidence that** girls are worse at Maths.
Older people **tend to** use less technology.
**I've met** a lot of relaxed people in the south.
slides.note: Useful words: **some**, **many**, **not all**, **tend to**, **often**, **in my experience**.

slides.title: Be fair
slides.instruction: Rewrite the generalisations to make them fairer.

items.q: All Americans eat fast food.
items.a: Some Americans eat a lot of fast food. (Not all Americans eat fast food.)

items.q: Boys never talk about their feelings.
items.a: Some boys find it hard to talk about their feelings.

items.q: People from Porto are always friendly.
items.a: In my experience, many people from Porto are friendly.

items.q: Gamers are antisocial.
items.a: Not all gamers are antisocial. Many play online with friends.

cards.heading: Who?
cards.text: Who wrote it? Is it a real news source or a random account?

cards.heading: When?
cards.text: Is it recent, or an old story shared again?

cards.heading: Evidence?
cards.text: Are there facts, numbers, sources? Can you find them elsewhere?

cards.heading: Why?
cards.text: Is it trying to make you angry or scared? Be careful.

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: What stereotypes do people have about teenagers?
Is there a stereotype about your town or region?
Can a stereotype ever be positive? Is it still a problem?
Have you ever shared something online that turned out to be false?
Where do stereotypes come from: films, family, social media?

slides.title: Remember
points: A **fact** can be checked; an **opinion** can't.

decks.title: Perfect Tenses
decks.subtitle: How long have you been waiting? What had happened?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: form and use the **present perfect continuous**
choose between **present perfect simple** and **continuous**
use the **past perfect** for the earlier of two past actions
tell a story with **when**, **after**, **before** and **by the time**

slides.title: Present perfect continuous: form
rows: Yes, I have. / No, he hasn't.
slides.note: With **How long...?** we use **for** (a period) and **since** (a starting point).

cards.heading: Still going on
cards.text: An action that started in the past and **continues now**.
cards.example: I've been learning English **for** six years.

cards.heading: Visible result
cards.text: An action that has **just stopped** and we can see the result.
cards.example: The street is wet. It's **been raining**.

cards.heading: Focus on duration
cards.text: We want to say **how long**, not how many.

slides.title: What have they been doing?
slides.instruction: Complete with the present perfect continuous of the verbs.

items.q: Your eyes are red. ___ you ___ (cry)?
I ___ (wait) for you for forty minutes!
Tomás ___ (play) Fortnite since lunch.
We ___ (not / sleep) well because of the heat.
How long ___ she ___ (learn) the guitar?
They're tired. They ___ (train) all morning.

left.heading: Present perfect simple
points: with **stative verbs**: know, like, want, belong

right.heading: Present perfect continuous
points: I**'ve been writing** emails all morning.
She**'s been reading** for two hours.

slides.title: Simple or continuous?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: I ___ this series since Friday. I'm on episode 6.
I ___ all eight episodes. What now?
He ___ his phone. Have you seen it?
We ___ each other for ten years.
You're all sweaty! ___ you ___ ?
She ___ three goals this season.

slides.title: Past perfect: form
slides.note: It's the same form for all persons: I **had**, he **had**, they **had**.

slides.title: Which happened first?
slides.text: Use the **past perfect** for the action that happened **first**, and the **past simple** for the later one. Compare:
examples: When I arrived, the bus **left**. (I saw it leave.)
When I arrived, the bus **had left**. (It left before. I missed it.)
**After** she **had finished** her homework, she went out.
**By the time** we got to the beach, it **had started** to rain.

slides.title: Join the sentences
slides.instruction: Join the sentences using the past perfect for the first action.

items.q: The match started. Then we got to the stadium. (When)
items.a: When we got to the stadium, the match had (already) started.

items.q: I studied for the test. Then I felt confident. (because)
items.a: I felt confident because I had studied for the test.

items.q: She saw the film. Then she read the book. (after)
items.a: She read the book after she had seen the film.

items.q: Everybody left. Then the police arrived. (By the time)
items.a: By the time the police arrived, everybody had left.

items.q: I never ate sushi before that night. (had never)
items.a: I had never eaten sushi before that night.

slides.title: A terrible start
text: Last Monday was a disaster. My alarm hadn't gone off because I had forgotten to charge my phone. When I finally woke up, my sister had already used all the hot water.
I ran to the bus stop, but the bus had left two minutes earlier. By the time I got to school, the Maths test had started. My teacher looked at me and said, "Nice of you to join us."
The worst part? I had studied for three days, and I knew every answer.

slides.title: Tell the story
slides.instruction: Complete with the past simple or the past perfect of the verbs.

items.q: When I ___ (wake up), my sister had used the hot water.
The bus ___ (leave) when I got to the stop.
My alarm ___ (not / go off) because my phone was dead.
By the time I ___ (arrive), the test had started.
I knew every answer because I ___ (study) a lot.
He ___ (never / be) so embarrassed before.

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: How long have you been learning English?
What have you been doing lately in your free time?
Tell us about a day when everything went wrong.
Had you ever been on a plane before you were ten?
What had you done before you came to class today?

slides.title: Remember
points: Present perfect simple for **results** and **how many**
Past perfect: **had** + past participle (the earlier past)

decks.title: Future Continuous & Perfect
decks.subtitle: This time next year, where will you be?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: use the **future continuous** for actions in progress in the future
use the **future perfect** for actions finished before a future time
use **by**, **by the time**, **this time next...** correctly
talk about your life in **ten years' time**

slides.title: Future continuous: form
rows: I**'ll be lying** on the beach.

cards.heading: A future snapshot
cards.text: An action **in progress** at a specific moment in the future.
cards.example: At 10 tomorrow, I**'ll be sitting** my exam.

cards.heading: Planned, routine
cards.text: Something that will happen as part of normal plans.
cards.example: I**'ll be passing** the shop, so I'll buy bread.

cards.heading: Polite questions
cards.text: Asking about plans without sounding pushy.

slides.title: This time tomorrow
slides.instruction: Complete with the future continuous of the verbs.

items.q: This time tomorrow, we ___ (fly) to London.
Don't call at 9. I ___ (have) my piano lesson.
___ you ___ (use) the car tonight, Dad?
In August, my cousins ___ (work) at a beach bar.
She ___ (not / study) on Saturday. It's her birthday.

slides.title: Future perfect: form
slides.note: We use it for an action that will be **complete before** a moment in the future.

slides.title: Time expressions
slides.text: **By** means 'not later than'. **By the time** + present simple. Never use **will** after **by the time**.
examples: **By** Friday, I'll have read the whole book.
**By the time** you **get** home, I'll have cooked dinner. (not: will get)
**In ten years' time**, we'll have finished university.
**This time next week**, we'll be skiing in Serra da Estrela.

slides.title: Before the deadline
slides.instruction: Complete with the future perfect of the verbs.

items.q: By June, we ___ (finish) 9.º ano.
By the time you arrive, the film ___ (start).
I ___ (not / save) enough money by Christmas.
___ they ___ (build) the stadium by 2030?
By the end of the year, she ___ (read) 50 books.

left.heading: Future continuous
points: the action is **happening** at that time
At 8 pm, I'**ll be doing** my homework.

right.heading: Future perfect
points: the action is **complete** before that time
By 8 pm, I'**ll have done** my homework.

slides.title: Which future?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: Don't phone at 3. We ___ lunch.
Phone at 4. We ___ lunch by then.
By the time I'm 30, I ___ married.
This time next month, I ___ in the sea.
By the time we ___ there, the shop will be closed.

items.en: In ten years' time, I**'ll have finished** university.
I**'ll be living** in a small flat in Porto, or maybe in Berlin.
I**'ll have learnt** to drive, but I probably **won't have bought** a car.
On a Monday morning, I**'ll be working** as a nurse at a hospital.
I hope I**'ll have travelled** to at least two other continents.

slides.title: Your future
slides.instruction: Answer about yourself. Use the future continuous or future perfect.

items.q: What will you be doing this time tomorrow?
items.a: This time tomorrow, I'll be sitting in my History class.

items.q: What will you have done by the end of this school year?
items.a: By the end of the year, I'll have finished 9.º ano and chosen my course for 10.º.

items.q: Where will you be living in ten years' time?
items.a: I'll be living in Lisbon, near the river.

items.q: What will you have learnt by the age of 25?
items.a: By the age of 25, I'll have learnt to cook properly and to drive.

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: What will you be doing at 9 pm on Saturday?
What will you have achieved by the time you're 20?
Where will you be spending your next summer holiday?
What will the world have changed by 2050?

slides.title: Remember
points: Future continuous: **will be** + -ing (in progress at a future time)
Future perfect: **will have** + past participle (finished before then)
**by** Friday, **by the time** + present simple, **in ten years' time**
**Will you be using...?** sounds polite and natural.

decks.title: Third Conditional and Wish
decks.subtitle: If I had known, I would have stayed in bed.

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: review the **first** and **second** conditionals
use the **third conditional** to imagine a different past
express wishes and regrets with **wish** and **if only**
talk about decisions you would change

slides.title: Conditionals at a glance
slides.note: The **if** clause can come first (use a comma) or second (no comma).

items.en: If I **had left** earlier, I **wouldn't have missed** the bus.
items.pt: (But I left late and I missed it.)

items.en: If Portugal **had scored** in the last minute, they **would have won**.
items.pt: (They didn't score, so they didn't win.)

items.en: She **would have passed** if she **had studied** a bit more.
If you **had told** me, I **would have helped** you.

slides.title: Careful with 'd
slides.text: In the third conditional, **'d** can mean **had** or **would**. Look at the next word: 'd + past participle = **had**; 'd + have = **would**.
examples: If I**'d** known... = If I **had** known...
...I**'d have** called you. = I **would have** called you.
Never use would in the if clause: If I **had** known (not: If I would have known)

slides.title: What if...?
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verbs (third conditional).

items.q: If we ___ (take) a taxi, we ___ (arrive) on time.
I ___ (not / fall) if I ___ (look) where I was going.
If she ___ (charge) her phone, she ___ (call) us.
They ___ (win) if the referee ___ (see) the foul.
If you ___ (not / shout), the dog ___ (not / run) away.

slides.title: One decision, two stories
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences using the third conditional.

items.q: I didn't set my alarm, so I was late.
items.a: If I had set my alarm, I wouldn't have been late.

items.q: He ate too much, so he felt sick.
items.a: If he hadn't eaten so much, he wouldn't have felt sick.

items.q: It rained, so we didn't go to the beach.
items.a: If it hadn't rained, we would have gone to the beach.

items.q: You didn't invite me, so I didn't come.
items.a: If you had invited me, I would have come.

slides.title: Wish and if only
rows: a present situation you want different
I wish I **hadn't eaten** that pizza.
annoyance: you want someone to change
an ability you'd like to have
slides.note: **If only** means the same as **I wish**, but it's stronger: **If only** I **had** more time!

slides.title: Be careful
slides.text: After wish, the verb goes one step **back** in time. With **be**, **were** is common for all persons. Don't use **would** to wish about yourself.
examples: I wish I **were** taller. (or: I wish I was taller.)
I wish I **knew** the answer. (now)
I wish I **had known** the answer. (in the test yesterday)
Not: I wish I would be taller.

slides.title: Wishes and regrets
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: I'm so tired. I wish I ___ to bed earlier last night.
I wish I ___ live near the beach. It's my dream.
I wish my brother ___ my clothes without asking!
If only I ___ the answer! The test is now.
She wishes she ___ that message. Now everyone has seen it.

slides.title: Make a wish
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences with I wish or If only.

items.q: I don't have a bike. (I wish)
items.a: I wish I had a bike.

items.q: I didn't go to the concert. (If only)
items.a: If only I had gone to the concert!

items.q: My neighbours always play loud music. (I wish)
items.a: I wish my neighbours wouldn't play loud music.

items.q: I can't swim very well. (I wish)
I'm not on holiday. (If only)
items.a: If only I were (was) on holiday!

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: What would have happened if you had been born in another country?
Is there a decision you wish you had made differently?
If you had lived 100 years ago, what would have been different?
Name one thing you wish you could do.
What do you wish people would stop doing on social media?

decks.title: The Passive Voice
decks.subtitle: It was made, it is being made, it will be made.

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: form the **passive** in all the main tenses
decide **when** to use the passive and when to add **by**
change active sentences into **passive** ones
describe a **process**: how pastéis de nata are made

cards.heading: Unknown agent
cards.text: We don't know who did it.

cards.heading: Obvious agent
cards.text: It's clear who did it, or it's not important.

cards.heading: Focus on the result
cards.text: The action or object matters more than the person.

cards.heading: Formal style
cards.text: News, science and instructions.

slides.title: be + past participle
slides.note: Only the verb **be** changes tense. The main verb is always the **past participle**.

slides.title: Which tense?
slides.instruction: Complete with the passive of the verb in the tense given.

items.q: The canteen ___ (paint) at the moment. (present cont.)
Over 100 emails ___ (send) every second. (present simple)
The match ___ (cancel) because of the storm. (past simple)
My phone ___ (steal)! Call the police! (present perfect)
The results ___ (publish) next week. (will)
Phones ___ (must / switch off) during exams.
The road ___ (repair) when we drove past. (past cont.)

slides.title: Do we need 'by'?
slides.text: Use **by** + agent only when the information is new or important. Don't use it with people, someone, they or obvious agents.
examples: Guernica was painted **by Picasso**. (important)
The thief was caught. (not: by the police)
English is spoken all over the world. (not: by people)

slides.title: Active to passive
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences in the passive. Use 'by' only if necessary.

items.q: Someone has broken the window.
José Saramago wrote Ensaio sobre a Cegueira.
items.a: Ensaio sobre a Cegueira was written by José Saramago.

items.q: They are building a new stadium in our town.
items.a: A new stadium is being built in our town.

items.q: The school will give a prize to the best project.
items.a: A prize will be given to the best project.

items.q: You can't use calculators in this test.
items.a: Calculators can't be used in this test.

slides.title: How pastéis de nata are made
text: First, the dough is rolled out very thin, spread with butter and folded several times. This is how puff pastry is made. Then it is rolled into a long tube and cut into small slices.
Each slice is pressed into a small metal tin with the thumbs, so the pastry goes up the sides. Next, the custard is prepared with milk, sugar, flour and egg yolks, and it is poured into the tins.
Finally, the tarts are baked in a very hot oven for a few minutes, until the tops are burnt in places. They are often eaten warm, with cinnamon and icing sugar on top.

slides.title: Put the process in order
slides.instruction: Put the words in order to make passive sentences about the recipe.

items.q: is / out / the / rolled / dough / thin
items.a: The dough is rolled out thin.

items.q: into / poured / is / custard / tins / the / the
items.a: The custard is poured into the tins.

items.q: tarts / a / baked / are / very / the / in / hot / oven
items.a: The tarts are baked in a very hot oven.

items.q: eaten / they / warm / often / are

slides.title: Passive quiz
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: The Mona Lisa ___ by Leonardo da Vinci.
Coffee ___ in Brazil and Colombia.
Your order ___ right now.
The winners ___ yet.
This problem ___ solved quickly.

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: What is your town known for? What is made or grown there?
Describe how your favourite dish is made, using the passive.
Have you ever had something stolen? What happened?
Which famous buildings in Portugal were built a long time ago?

slides.title: Remember
points: is **being** made, has **been** made, will **be** made, must **be** made
Use the passive when the **action** is more important than the person.
Add **by** + agent only when it's useful information.

decks.title: Reported Speech
decks.subtitle: She said she would call. She didn't.

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: report what people **said**, moving tenses **back**
change words for **time** and **place**
report **questions** with the right word order
report **commands** and **requests** with tell and ask

slides.title: Statements: tenses go back
rows: He said he **was watching** a film.
He said he **had seen** the match.
slides.note: Pronouns change too: "**I** love **your** dog" becomes She said **she** loved **my** dog.

right.heading: tell
points: **tell** a story, a lie, the truth, a joke

slides.title: Say or tell?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: Rita ___ me she was moving to Faro.
He ___ that the test was easy.
Don't ___ lies to your parents!
What did she ___ to you?
Grandad ___ us a funny story about the army.

slides.title: Time and place words
slides.note: These change only if the time or place is different when we report the words.

slides.title: What did they say?
slides.instruction: Report the statements. Start with the words given.

items.q: "I'm going to the beach tomorrow." Inês said...
items.a: Inês said (that) she was going to the beach the next day.

items.q: "We lost the match yesterday." They told me...
items.a: They told me (that) they had lost the match the day before.

items.q: "I can't find my keys." Dad said...
items.a: Dad said (that) he couldn't find his keys.

items.q: "I'll help you with your project." Ana told me...
items.a: Ana told me (that) she would help me with my project.

items.q: "I've never been to London." Rui said...
items.a: Rui said (that) he had never been to London.

slides.title: Reported questions
slides.text: Reported questions are **not** questions: use normal word order (subject + verb), no **do/does/did** and no question mark. Yes/no questions use **if** or **whether**.
examples: "Where **do you live**?" → She asked me where **I lived**.
"What time **is it**?" → He asked what time **it was**.
"**Are you** coming?" → They asked **if I was** coming.
"**Did you** like it?" → Mum asked **whether I had** liked it.

slides.title: Report the questions
slides.instruction: Report the questions. Start with the words given.

items.q: "Where are you from?" The tourist asked me...
items.a: The tourist asked me where I was from.

items.q: "Do you like sushi?" Leo asked her...
items.a: Leo asked her if (whether) she liked sushi.

items.q: "Why did you leave early?" The teacher asked us...
items.a: The teacher asked us why we had left early.

items.q: "Have you seen my charger?" My sister asked me...
items.a: My sister asked me if (whether) I had seen her charger.

items.q: "What will you do in the summer?" Gran asked me...
items.a: Gran asked me what I would do in the summer.

items.en: "Sit down!" → The teacher **told us to sit** down.
"Don't touch my phone!" → She **told me not to touch** her phone.
"Can you close the window, please?" → He **asked me to close** the window.
"Please don't be late." → Mum **asked us not to be** late.

slides.title: Orders and favours
slides.instruction: Complete the reported commands and requests.

items.q: "Turn off the TV." Dad told me ___ the TV.
"Don't run in the corridor!" She told us ___ in the corridor.
"Could you lend me a pen?" He asked me ___ him a pen.
"Don't forget your passport." Mum ___ me not to forget my passport.
"Please wait here." The nurse asked us ___ there.

slides.title: Let's talk
questions: What's the best advice anyone has ever given you? Report it.
What did your parents tell you to do this morning?
What did your best friend ask you last time you met?
Report a funny thing someone said to you this week.

slides.title: Remember
points: Tenses go back: am → **was**, saw → **had seen**, will → **would**
Questions: **asked** + if / wh- word + subject + verb

decks.title: Relative Clauses
decks.subtitle: The friend who, the place where, the day when.

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: use **who**, **which**, **that**, **whose**, **where** and **when**
tell the difference between **defining** and **non-defining** clauses
know when to use **commas** and when you can leave out the pronoun
join two sentences into one, more natural sentence

slides.title: Relative pronouns
rows: the girl **who** sits next to me
the boy **whose** dad is a pilot
