story.title: Thursday Nights
story.subtitle: A river, a school project and a secret that someone wants to keep
story.blurb: Inês and her friends only wanted to put a few cheap sensors in their town's brown river for a school project. Then, at three o'clock one Thursday morning, sensor seven goes crazy and switches itself off. Someone in Ribeira Alta has a secret, and someone else, who calls themselves Kestrel, wants them to find it.

characters.name: Inês Pacheco
characters.desc: is fourteen and wants to be an environmental engineer. She is organised, stubborn and asks too many questions.

characters.name: Tomás Reis
characters.desc: is her best friend. He can fix almost anything with tape and a screwdriver, and he never stops joking, even when he is scared.

characters.name: Priya Nair
characters.desc: moved from Kochi, in India, to Ribeira Alta the year before. She speaks three languages, writes code and does not suffer fools.

characters.name: Matilde Viana
characters.desc: is the daughter of the owner of the local dye works. Everyone thinks they know who she is.

characters.name: Avô Zé
characters.desc: is Tomás's grandfather. He worked at the dye works for thirty-one years and remembers things the town would prefer to forget.

characters.name: Ms Sousa
characters.desc: is their English teacher. She runs the WaterWatch project and is very hard to say no to.

chapters.title: Sensor Number Seven
paragraphs: The river smelt of rain and diesel on the first day of school. Inês Pacheco stopped on the old stone bridge with one foot on the ground and looked down at the water. It was brown and slow, the colour of cold tea. She had been crossing this bridge every school day since she was six, and she had never once seen the bottom.
"You're doing it again," said Tomás Reis, braking next to her with a noise like an angry seagull. His bike was older than both of them. "Staring at the river like it owes you money."
"Somebody owes the river money," said Inês. "Look at it."
"I've been looking at it for fifteen years. Rivers are brown. Come on, we'll be late, and Ms Sousa has been planning something all summer."

Ribeira Alta was a small town on the River Ave, half an hour from Porto by train. It had a church, two cafés, a football pitch with more mud than grass, and the long grey walls of the Viana dye works, which had been colouring cloth for clothing brands since Tomás's grandfather was a boy. On some days the whole town smelt faintly of hot, wet fabric. Nobody talked about it much.
Ms Sousa was waiting in room 12 with a look on her face that meant extra work.

"Good morning, 9.ºB. Phones away. I'm only going to explain this once." She turned the laptop round. On the screen there was a map with three red dots: one in the north of Portugal, one at the southern tip of Africa and one far away in the South Pacific. "This year our school is taking part in WaterWatch. Schools in three countries are going to build cheap sensors, put them in their local rivers and share the data online. Our partners are a school in Cape Town, in South Africa, and a school in Wellington, in New Zealand."
"Do they speak Portuguese?" asked Duarte from the back.

"No, Duarte, and we don't speak isiXhosa or Māori. Some of them speak English at home and some don't. It doesn't matter. English is the language we all share, so everything will be in English." "By June, you will have collected more information about this river than anyone in this town has ever collected. And you will have presented it, live, to a jury on the other side of the world."
Inês had her hand up before she had decided to put it up. Next to her, Tomás groaned.

Ms Sousa wanted teams of four. Inês wrote her own name on the board, then Tomás's, without asking him. The third name surprised everyone. Priya Nair, who sat alone by the window and had hardly said a word since she had arrived from Kochi, in the south of India, the year before, walked to the board, wrote her name in neat capital letters and went back to her seat.

"I've been teaching myself to code for two years," she said quietly when Inês turned round to look at her. "You'll need someone to build the website. He can't do it." She pointed at Tomás with her pen.
"How do you know I can't?"
"I've seen your Instagram."
The fourth place stayed empty until Ms Sousa filled it herself. "Matilde, you'll join this group."
Matilde Viana looked up from her phone. Everybody knew Matilde: the expensive trainers, the perfect hair, the father who owned the dye works.
"I didn't sign up for anything," she said.
"I know," said Ms Sousa. "That's why I signed you up."
That afternoon there was a careers session in the library. A woman from a technology company in Porto asked everyone to write down where they would be in ten years.
"This time in ten years," Inês read out, "I'll be working as an environmental engineer. I'll have finished my degree, and I'll be cleaning up rivers like this one."
"This time in ten years I'll be fixing your equipment," said Tomás, "because you'll have broken it."
Priya didn't read hers out, but Inês saw it anyway. I will have started my own company. I will be living wherever I want.
Matilde's paper was blank. When the woman asked her about it, she shrugged. "I'll be doing whatever my father has already decided."

The first video call took place two weeks later, at ten in the morning. In Cape Town it was eleven. In Wellington it was ten at night, and Aroha, the girl who led the New Zealand team, was wearing pyjamas with little sheep on them.
"Don't say anything," she warned. "My mum bought them."

Thandi, from Cape Town, had a laugh you could hear from the corridor. When Tomás asked about batteries, she promised to send him the details "just now", and he waited by the screen for five minutes before Priya explained that in South Africa "just now" can mean "later, maybe in an hour". Aroha said that everything was "sweet as". Ms Sousa wrote both expressions on the board.
"Nobody speaks English in exactly the same way," she said after the call. "That's what makes it useful. You don't have to sound like the King. You have to make yourself understood."

For the rest of September, the team spent every afternoon in the garage of Tomás's grandfather. Avô Zé had worked at the dye works for thirty-one years and now spent his days growing tomatoes and complaining about football. He watched them build the sensors out of plastic pipes, cheap circuit boards and a lot of tape.
"In my day," he said, "we didn't need machines to tell us what was in the river. We could see it. Red on Mondays, blue on Thursdays."
"Is that true?" asked Priya.
"Ask anyone over sixty." He tapped his nose. "But that was a long time ago. They cleaned everything up. Now they've got a treatment plant and inspectors and all that."

Matilde came to the garage twice. She turned out to be surprisingly good at soldering, but she never stayed longer than an hour, and she kept checking her phone, as if somebody was keeping an eye on her.

On the first Saturday of October they set up the seven sensors along three kilometres of river, from the bridge down to the old fishing pier below the dye works. Sensor number seven went in last. Tomás tied it to a wooden post of the pier with a double knot he was very proud of, a few metres from a wide concrete pipe that came out of the bank and disappeared under the water.
"What's that pipe for?" asked Inês.
"Rain water, I think," said Matilde, and turned away.

Priya switched the sensors on one by one from her laptop. Seven green dots appeared on the map. Every ten minutes the website showed new numbers: the temperature, the pH and how cloudy the water was. For a week, nothing interesting happened. Tomás started calling it the most boring website in Europe.
Then, at twenty past three on a Friday morning, Inês's phone buzzed on her bedside table. It was Priya.
Wake up. Look at sensor seven.

Inês opened the website with her eyes half closed. Six green dots, and one grey one. At 3.02, the temperature next to the pier had jumped by nine degrees. At 3.12, the pH had shot up to a level that the website showed in red. The line for cloudy water went straight off the top of the graph.
At 3.19, sensor seven had stopped sending anything at all.
Another message arrived.
Sensors don't switch themselves off. Somebody has switched it off.

chapters.title: Kestrel
paragraphs: They were at the pier by half past seven, before the mist had lifted from the water. Matilde hadn't answered any of their messages, so there were only three of them: Inês, still wearing her pyjama top under her jacket, Tomás with a bag of tools he didn't need, and Priya holding her laptop against her chest like a shield.
The wooden post was still there. So was the rope, with Tomás's famous double knot. But the end of the rope had been cut cleanly, with something sharp. Sensor seven had gone.
"Maybe it fell," said Tomás. Nobody answered him. Ropes don't cut themselves either.

Inês walked along the edge of the pier. The concrete pipe was quiet now, with only a thin line of water coming out of it. But the stones around it were stained a strange dark purple, and the mud smelt sharp and chemical, like the inside of a new pair of jeans. She took photos of everything. Her hands were so cold that the first few came out blurred.
"Somebody had been here before us," Priya said. "Look."

In the soft ground at the end of the old service road there were tyre marks, wide ones, from something much heavier than a car. They came down the road, turned and stopped next to a round metal cover in the ground: an old drain.
"A lorry," said Tomás. "A big one. Reversing."

By the time they got to school, the first lesson had already started. At break they told Ms Sousa everything. She listened without interrupting, then said, "Write it all down. Times, photos, everything. Don't touch anything, and don't go down there at night. Is that clear?"
"Clear," said Inês. Tomás didn't say anything at all.
Matilde finally appeared at lunch. She sat down at their table in the canteen, which she had never done before, and listened while Priya showed her the graph.

"My father's factory has been inspected every year since before I was born," she said when Priya had finished. "They've got a treatment plant. They've got cameras. You've been watching too many documentaries."
"We're not saying it's the factory," said Inês. "We're saying something happened at three in the morning next to your father's factory, and then somebody cut our sensor off a rope."
Matilde looked at her for a long moment. Then she picked up her tray and left. She didn't come to the garage that week, or the week after.
It was Avô Zé who gave them their first real piece of information. He listened to the whole story while he was tying up his tomato plants, and then he sat down slowly on an upturned box.

"In 1989," he said, "I was working the night shift. One night I went outside for a cigarette and I saw a lorry parked by that old drain on the service road. They had connected a hose and they were emptying something into it. I had never seen that lorry before, and nobody had told us anything. The next morning, the river was black from the pier to the bridge."
"What did you do?" asked Priya.

"I told my boss. He told me I had dreamt it." Avô Zé shrugged. "I had a wife, two children and a job. I didn't make a fuss. But I've been thinking about that lorry for more than thirty years." He pointed with his chin towards the river. "That drain goes straight into the big pipe by the pier. It's for rain water. Or it's supposed to be."

They didn't give up. Tomás came up with a smaller sensor that could be hidden inside an old plastic bottle. Priya set up a system that saved the data in two places at once, just in case. Inês looked into who used the service road and found out that nobody was supposed to: it belonged to the town council and had been closed to traffic for years. By the end of October, a new sensor was sitting in the water under the pier, where nobody on the bank could see it.
For three weeks nothing happened. Then, on a Tuesday evening in November, Priya called the other two on a video call. She had been staring at her screen for so long that her eyes were red.
"Somebody has written to us," she said. "On the WaterWatch platform."

The message had come through the project chat, where students from all three schools could write to each other. The sender's profile had no school, no country and no photo, just a small drawing of a bird of prey with its wings spread. The username was Kestrel.
You've been looking at the wrong thing. It isn't the factory. Watch the drain on the service road. Thursday nights, after 2 a.m. Don't go alone. And don't tell anyone about this message.
"Who is Kestrel?" asked Tomás. "Someone from Cape Town? From Wellington?"
Priya had already asked. Thandi promised it wasn't anyone from her school. Aroha said she had asked her whole team and they were "as confused as a cat in a bath".
"The English is perfect," said Inês.

"That means nothing," said Priya. "Millions of people write perfect English online. My grandmother in Kochi writes better English than half the politicians on TV. It could be anybody. It could be someone in this town."
"Someone who knows about the lorry," said Inês.
They looked at each other through their three small screens. Inês knew exactly what Tomás was going to say before he said it.
"Thursday's the day after tomorrow."
"Ms Sousa said..."

"Ms Sousa said not to go down there at night. Kestrel said not to go alone. There are three of us." He grinned. "By Friday morning we'll either have found something, or we'll have been grounded until we're thirty."

On Thursday night, Inês lay in bed fully dressed until the house was quiet. At ten to two she climbed out of her window onto the garage roof, the way she had been doing since she was eleven, and slid down the drainpipe. Tomás was waiting at the end of the street with his bike and no lights. Priya met them at the bridge, wearing a black coat that was three sizes too big for her.
"My father's," she whispered. "He thinks I'm asleep."

They hid behind an old fishing boat that had been lying upside down on the bank for years. The river made small sucking noises against the pier. It was cold enough to see their breath. At half past two nothing had happened. By quarter to three Tomás had started complaining about his feet.
At 2.52, headlights came down the service road.

A tanker lorry with no name on its side reversed slowly towards the drain. Its lights went off for the last twenty metres. A man climbed down from the cab. He was big, and he moved quickly, like someone who had done this many times before. He lifted the metal cover, pulled a thick hose from the back of the tanker and pushed one end into the drain. Then he turned a handle, and the night filled with the sound of liquid rushing away underground.
Tomás had his phone out. The screen glowed a tiny, terrible blue.
"Turn it down," Inês hissed.
Too late. A torch beam swung across the bank, across the boat, and stopped on Inês's face.
"Hey!" shouted the man. "Who's there?"

chapters.title: The Phone in the Mud
paragraphs: They ran.

Afterwards, Inês could never remember which way they had gone first. She remembered the torch beam jumping over the grass, the man's heavy boots behind them, and Priya's huge coat flapping like a flag. She remembered Tomás slipping on the wet stones and falling hard on one knee. His phone flew out of his hand and landed somewhere in the mud, its screen still glowing.
"Leave it!" Inês grabbed his arm and pulled him up.

The man was close enough now for them to hear his breathing. Then Priya did something none of them expected. She turned round, pointed her own phone at him and switched on the flash. For one second the man stopped, his arm over his eyes. One second was enough. They threw themselves through a gap in the fence, ran between the bare vines of Senhor Abel's vineyard and came out on the main road. They kept running until they reached the bus shelter by the church.
Nobody had followed them. They sat on the cold plastic bench, breathing in great painful gulps, and for a long time nobody said anything.
"My phone," said Tomás at last. "My phone's down there."
"Your knee's bleeding," said Priya.
"My mum's going to kill me. Not because of the knee. Because of the phone."
Inês got home at ten past four, climbed back up the drainpipe and lay in bed with her heart beating so loudly that she was sure her parents could hear it through the wall. She didn't sleep at all.

At school the next day the three of them looked like extras from a zombie film. Priya had been up since six, checking the data. The hidden sensor under the pier had survived. At 2.58 it had recorded the same pattern as in October: the temperature jumped, the pH shot up and the water became so cloudy that the line went off the screen.
"So now we've got numbers," she said. "But numbers aren't a lorry. Anyone can say our sensor's broken."
"We had a video," said Tomás miserably. "I was recording the whole time."
Priya sat up. "Is your phone set to back up to the cloud?"
"I think so. My cousin set it up. Why?"

"Because if it's still switched on, and if somebody takes it somewhere with Wi-Fi, the video will upload automatically." She was already typing. "I'm setting up an alert on your account. The second anything arrives, we'll know."
"It's lying in the mud next to a river," said Inês. "By tonight the battery will have died."
"Probably," said Priya. "But probably isn't certainly."

Nothing arrived. Not that day, not that week. Tomás told his mother that he had lost his phone at football, which she believed for exactly as long as it took her to find his muddy jeans in the washing machine. He wasn't allowed out in the evenings until Christmas. Inês felt so guilty that she took him a box of pastéis de nata every Saturday, and he ate them all in front of her without offering her one.
They went back to the pier once, in daylight, with Ms Sousa's permission and Avô Zé as a bodyguard. The phone had gone. So had the tyre marks. Somebody had raked the mud flat.
"Somebody's been tidying up," said Avô Zé quietly. "In my day they never bothered."

That night Priya wrote to Kestrel on the WaterWatch chat. We went. We saw the lorry. Who are you, and what do you know? The message was marked as read eleven minutes later. No answer came, not that night and not in the weeks that followed. Every evening Inês checked the chat before she went to sleep, and every evening the little bird with its wings spread said nothing at all.

December came. The town council put up the same Christmas lights as every year, a long line of blue stars across the main street that made the town look, Tomás said, like a cheap casino. The WaterWatch teams had their last video call of the term on the Friday before the holidays. Thandi's team had found a broken sewage pipe near a beach and had already written to the city council about it. Aroha's team had been testing water from dairy farms after heavy rain. Both teams had photos, letters and plans.
Then it was Ribeira Alta's turn. Priya shared the graph with its two huge spikes. The project coordinator, a calm man in Edinburgh called Dr Fraser, leaned towards his camera.
"Those are remarkable readings," he said. "What's causing them?"
Inês looked at Tomás. Tomás looked at the floor.
"We think somebody is dumping chemicals into a drain at night," she said. "We saw it happen. But we haven't got any proof yet."
"Then that's your job for next term," said Dr Fraser. "Remember: in June you won't just be showing us graphs. You'll be explaining them. And if you can't prove something, don't say it."
"This time next term," said Inês gloomily after the call, "we'll be standing in front of that jury with nothing."
"This time next term," said Priya, "we'll have found something. We've got six months."
"Five and a half," said Tomás.

Matilde had stopped coming to their meetings completely. At the school Christmas concert she sat in the second row next to her father, a tall grey man in a dark coat who clapped politely at everything. Once, during the choir, Inês turned round and caught Matilde looking at her. Matilde looked away first.

On the evening of the twenty-third of December, Inês was at her grandmother's flat in Porto, wrapping presents with the TV on, when her phone started vibrating and didn't stop. Twelve messages from Priya, one after another.
IT UPLOADED.
The video. Tomás's video. 11.58 p.m.
Call me NOW.
Inês locked herself in the bathroom and called. Priya answered before the first ring had finished.
"Where was the phone?" Inês whispered. "Where did it upload from?"
"That's the strange part. It connected to a Wi-Fi network called VIANA-OFFICE."
Inês sat down on the edge of the bath. "The dye works."
"Watch the video first. Watch it to the end."

Priya sent the link, and Inês pressed play. The picture was dark and shaky: the lorry, the hose, the man's back, a number plate that the torch lit up for less than a second. Then shouting, the picture spinning, a long confused blur, and then mud. The phone was lying on its side, still recording, filming a sideways world of grass and black water.

For almost a minute nothing happened. Then there were footsteps. Somebody small and light walked into the picture, bent down and picked the phone up. For one second the screen lit their face from below.
A red coat. Long dark hair, wet with rain. A face Inês had seen almost every day for nine years.
She watched it three times, just to be sure. There was no mistake.
It was Matilde.

chapters.title: The Red Coat
paragraphs: Matilde didn't answer the phone over Christmas. She didn't answer messages either. Inês watched the two grey ticks under her messages for ten days, and they never turned blue.
On the first day of the second term, Inês found her in the library, alone at the table behind the encyclopaedias, where nobody ever sat because the radiator didn't work.
"You were there," said Inês. She put her phone on the table, with the video paused on Matilde's face. "That night at the pier. You took Tomás's phone."
Matilde looked at the screen for a long time. Her face didn't change, but her fingers closed slowly round her pen.
"Delete that," she said.
"Why were you there? Why did you take it? Why did it upload from your father's office?"

"I said delete it." Matilde stood up. Her voice was low and hard. "You have no idea what you're doing. If you'd stayed at home that night, like normal people, none of this would have happened. If Tomás hadn't been filming, that man wouldn't have seen you. You were lucky. Do you understand? You were very lucky."
"Who was he, Matilde?"
"Stay away from the river," said Matilde, and walked out. The librarian looked up and said "Shh!" to Inês, who hadn't said anything.

That week, in Citizenship, their teacher Mr Lobo started a project on consumption. He asked everyone to look at the labels inside their clothes. Tomás found that his hoodie had been made in Bangladesh, designed in Sweden and sold in a shopping centre in Matosinhos.
"Your hoodie has travelled more than you have," said Priya.

"A lot of the clothes we buy are only worn a few times," said Mr Lobo, "and then they're thrown away. They're designed to be cheap and fast. But somebody has to dye them, and dyeing cloth uses enormous amounts of water and chemicals. So where does all that dirty water go?"
Several people turned to look at Matilde. She kept her eyes on her notebook.

"In a good factory," Mr Lobo went on, "the water is cleaned before it's returned to the river. In a bad one, it isn't. And the cheaper the clothes are, the more pressure there is to save money somewhere."
At break, Tomás stood looking at his new trainers as if they had insulted him. "I wish I hadn't bought these," he said. "If I'd known all this, I would have bought the other ones."
"The other ones were made in the same factory," said Priya.
"If only you'd told me that in August."

That evening Inês went through her wardrobe. She found eleven T-shirts, although she only ever wore four of them. Some had been bought in the sales because they were cheap; others because her friends had the same ones. She put the ones she never wore into a bag so that she could take them to the charity shop on Monday. It didn't feel like much. Still, it was something, and it stopped her thinking about Matilde's face on that little screen for almost an hour.

On the third Saturday of January, Inês was woken by her mother calling her to the kitchen. The local news was on the radio. Hundreds of dead fish had been found along the banks of the Ave, between the bridge and the pier. Samples of water had been collected by the environmental authorities that morning, the reporter said, and the results would be published in the coming weeks.

Inês didn't wait for the results. She cycled to the bridge. Half the town was already there, standing in their coats and looking down at the river. The fish lay on the mud in long silver lines, their eyes white. The smell was terrible. Somebody's dog was barking and wouldn't stop.
Priya's data showed exactly what they had all expected: another spike on a Thursday night, at 3.06 a.m.
"It's him," said Tomás. "The lorry man. It's the same pattern."
"We know that," said Priya. "Nobody else does."

By lunchtime, somebody else had an explanation. It appeared on Ribeira Alta Unida, a Facebook group with four thousand members, where people usually complained about potholes and lost cats. The post had been written by Carlos Mota, who owned a waste transport company on the edge of town and always had something to say at every town meeting.

Has anybody noticed that the river got worse when the new laundry opened? Hundreds of litres of soap and chemicals every day, and nobody checks. These people come here, they don't follow our rules, and we pay the price. It's time somebody asked questions.

He hadn't written a name. He didn't need to. There was only one new laundry in Ribeira Alta: Rajan's Wash and Dry, which Priya's uncle had opened in the summer in an old garage near the river. It washed towels for two hotels and the clothes of half the university students who rented rooms in town.
By the evening the post had been shared more than three hundred times. Underneath it there were comments that Inês read once and then wished she had never read at all.

"My uncle washes towels," said Priya. She was sitting on the floor of Avô Zé's garage with her knees under her chin. "With soap. The water goes into the town sewers, like everybody else's. He's had every licence checked twice, because he knew people would be watching him."
"Then it'll be fine," said Tomás. "Anyone can see it isn't him."
"Anyone could see it if they looked," said Priya. "But nobody's looking. They don't want to look. They've already decided."
"If we'd shown everyone the video in December," said Inês, "this wouldn't be happening."
"If we'd shown the video in December," said Priya, "everyone would be talking about Matilde, and the man in the lorry would have hidden everything. You can't see his face. You can only see hers."
Inês knew she was right, and she hated it. She wished she could go back to the night at the pier and run towards the lorry instead of away from it.
Avô Zé had been listening from his armchair. He said nothing, but Inês noticed that he had stopped pretending to read his newspaper.
On Sunday morning, at seven o'clock, Priya rang. She didn't say hello. In the background Inês could hear a man speaking very fast in a language she didn't understand, and a woman crying.
"Come to the laundry," said Priya. "Please. Now."

Inês got there in twelve minutes. A small crowd had gathered on the pavement. The big front window of Rajan's Wash and Dry had been smashed, and pieces of glass were lying all over the clean white floor, between the washing machines. A stone the size of a fist lay next to the counter. Priya's uncle was standing in the middle of it all in his slippers, holding a broom he hadn't started to use.
And across the metal door, in red paint that was still wet enough to run, someone had sprayed three words.
GO BACK HOME.

chapters.title: Volunteers
paragraphs: The police came, wrote some notes and left. A man from the insurance company came, took photographs and left. Priya's uncle Rajan swept up the glass himself, slowly and carefully, and wouldn't let anybody help him.
Priya didn't come to school on Monday or Tuesday. On Wednesday she came back, sat at her desk by the window and didn't speak to anyone, except to say "present" when her name was called.

It was Ms Sousa who changed things, although she did it so quietly that nobody noticed at first. In English that week, instead of the next unit in the book, she gave them a single page: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which was adopted by the United Nations in 1948. She read it out loud.
"All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights."

Then she asked them what "dignity" meant. Nobody could explain it, so she asked for examples instead. Duarte said dignity was not being laughed at. Leonor said it was being called by your real name. Tomás said it was not having to prove you were innocent every time something went wrong. Ms Sousa wrote all their answers on the board and didn't add anything.

At the end of the lesson Priya put her hand up for the first time that week. "In Kochi," she said, "nobody looked at me twice. Here I'm always the Indian girl. Even when people are being nice, I'm the Indian girl. I'm not complaining. I'm just saying that sometimes I would like to be Priya."
Nobody laughed. Nobody said anything clever. The bell rang, and for once nobody ran for the door.
That afternoon, in the garage, Inês had an idea. "We need to do something people can see," she said. "Not posts. Not comments. Something real."

The something real took three weeks to organise. Inês wrote to the parish council. Tomás talked to the scouts, who had a van and a lot of gloves. Priya designed posters in Portuguese and in English, because there were students from Brazil, Ukraine and Nepal at their school and she wanted them to know they were invited too. The plan was simple. On the last Saturday of February, the town would clean the riverbank from the bridge to the pier. On the way back, everybody would stop at Rajan's Wash and Dry, where the new window was going to be put in that same morning, and have a free coffee.
"The river isn't his fault," said Tomás. "But people need a reason to go and meet him, so we're giving them one."
"Free coffee is a very good reason," said Inês.

By the Friday before, almost everything had been arranged. Gloves and bags would be provided by the parish council. The rubbish would be collected in the scouts' van and taken to the recycling centre. Water samples were going to be taken by a biology lecturer from the University of Porto, who had seen Priya's graph on the WaterWatch website and had written to ask if she could come. Posters had been put up in both cafés, in the church and even in the window of the pharmacy.
On the school noticeboard, under one of the posters, somebody had written in pencil: Who's paying for this? The Indians? Inês rubbed it out with her thumb and didn't tell Priya.

On Saturday morning it rained. Inês stood on the bridge at nine o'clock with a box of gloves, certain that nobody would come. By half past nine there were forty people. By ten there were more than a hundred: students, grandparents, the scouts, the under-15 football team, the woman from the bakery, and Avô Zé with three of his old friends from the dye works, all of them wearing their old work boots.
And Matilde.

She arrived alone, in old jeans and a grey jacket that nobody had ever seen her wear. She picked up a bag, walked to the dirtiest part of the bank and started working without saying a word to anyone. She didn't stop for three hours. She pulled out plastic bottles, a car tyre, a shopping trolley and something that might once have been a sofa. People stared at her. She didn't seem to notice.
"In spite of everything," said Tomás, watching her, "I quite like her."
"You like anyone who can carry a sofa," said Inês.

Around eleven, a woman Inês recognised from the Facebook group walked over to Priya's uncle, who was dragging a heavy bag of bottles up the bank. She had been one of the first people to share Carlos Mota's post. For a moment the two of them just looked at each other. Then she took the other side of the bag, and they carried it up to the van together without a word. It wasn't an apology. But, as Priya said later, it wasn't nothing either.
Carlos Mota didn't come. One of his lorries drove past on the main road twice during the morning, and the second time the driver hooted at the volunteers. Some people waved back. Inês didn't.

By lunchtime more than two hundred bags of rubbish had been collected. Most of it was plastic, but a lot of it was clothes: socks, T-shirts, even a whole bag of jeans that somebody had thrown into the river instead of taking them to a recycling bin. The biology lecturer filled twelve small bottles with water and mud and labelled each one carefully.
"These will be analysed in our lab next week," she told Inês. "If there's something in this river that shouldn't be there, it will be found. I can promise you that."
They were almost at the pier when Tomás, who had been walking in the shallow water in his grandfather's fishing boots, suddenly stopped. His left boot had sunk into the mud up to the knee.
"There's something down here," he said. "Something hard."

He reached into the water and pulled, and pulled again. With a long sucking sound, something came out of the mud: a short white plastic tube, scratched and covered in black slime, with a cut piece of rope still tied to one end.
Sensor seven.
"It's been lying here all this time," said Priya. "They just threw it into the river."

But Inês was looking at the other end of the tube. The cap was on, but it was clean, much cleaner than the rest. Somebody had unscrewed it and screwed it back on, and not long ago. Tomás opened it. Inside, wrapped in a small plastic bag, there was a memory card.
It wasn't theirs.
The bag was dry and new. Whatever had been lying in the mud since October, this hadn't. Somebody had put it there for them to find, maybe only the night before.
And on the plastic, in black marker, somebody had drawn a small bird with its wings spread.

chapters.title: What the Card Remembered
paragraphs: They opened the memory card that evening in Priya's kitchen, while her mother made tea that nobody drank. There were forty-three photos on it. Most of them were photos of documents, taken quickly and a little crooked, as if the person holding the camera had been listening for footsteps.

The first ones were waste transport forms. Every Thursday, for more than a year, the Viana dye works had paid a company called MotaTrans to collect twenty thousand litres of dye waste. According to the forms, the waste was taken to a treatment plant near Porto, where it was supposed to be cleaned. Every form had been signed by the same person: C. Mota.
"Carlos Mota," said Tomás. "The man from the Facebook group."

The next photo was a printed email from the treatment plant. Inês read it twice to make sure she had understood the English, then the Portuguese version underneath. In answer to your question, it said, we confirm that no deliveries from MotaTrans have been received at this plant since last March.
Nobody spoke for a moment. Priya's mother put down the teapot.

"So the factory pays him to take the waste to the plant," said Inês slowly, "but the waste never gets there. He drives it down the service road, empties it into the drain at three in the morning and keeps the money."
"And then he tells the whole town that my uncle is poisoning the river," said Priya. Her voice was very calm, which was worse than if she had shouted. "So that nobody looks at him."

The last photos had been taken at night, from a window high above the service road. They showed the tanker, the hose and the drain. In one of them the light inside the cab was on, and a man was sitting behind the wheel, looking at his phone. His face was perfectly clear.
It was Carlos Mota.
"If he had done it somewhere else," said Tomás, "in a river nobody cared about, nobody would ever have noticed."
"Somebody always cares about a river," said Priya's mother quietly, in English. It was the first thing she had said all evening.
Later that night, Tomás showed the photo to Avô Zé. The old man looked at it for a long time, holding the phone at arm's length because he had forgotten his glasses.

"MotaTrans," he said at last. "When his father ran it, it was called Transportes Mota. Same blue lorries." He gave the phone back. "In 1989 I never saw the driver's face. I've always wished I had gone closer."
The next question was harder. Who had taken the photos? Whoever Kestrel was, they had been inside the office of the dye works, and they had been watching the service road from one of its windows.
"Matilde," said Inês. "It has to be."
"Or her father," said Tomás. "Think about it. If he knew about Mota, sending us after him would be the perfect way to make himself look innocent."
Inês didn't like that idea, but she couldn't say it was impossible.

Two weeks later, the results from the University of Porto arrived. Traces of industrial dyes had been found in the mud next to the pier. The water near the laundry had been tested too, and it was no worse than in any other part of a town river. The biology lecturer sent them a long, careful report in which she explained every number.

On Sunday they had a video call with Cape Town and Wellington. Thandi listened to the whole story and then said, "When we found our sewage pipe, our teacher told us one thing: take it to the people whose job it is. Not to Facebook. Not to the newspapers. Not first."

"We nearly made that mistake," said Aroha. "Last year we found a farm that was letting waste into a stream. If we'd posted the photos online, the farmer would have cleaned everything up before anybody official came. We took them to the regional council instead, and they caught him."

So they went to Ms Sousa, and Ms Sousa went with Inês's mother to the GNR post in the next town, where there was a sergeant from the environmental protection unit. Sergeant Costa was a short woman with tired eyes who read every page without saying a word. Then she made copies of everything.

"This will be investigated," she said. "Properly. That means slowly. I can't tell you what we're doing, and you mustn't tell anybody what you've given us. Do you understand? If he finds out what we know, the evidence could be destroyed before we get to it."
"How long will it take?" asked Inês.
"As long as it takes."

It took a long time. Inês checked the news every morning, as if the answer might suddenly appear there. March went by. The fruit trees in Avô Zé's garden came into flower. MotaTrans lorries drove up and down the main road as usual, and on Thursday nights Priya's hidden sensor recorded nothing at all, as if somebody had decided to be careful for a while.

At Rajan's Wash and Dry the new window shone, but the customers were fewer every week. One of the hotels had found another laundry. Priya's uncle started talking about moving to Lisbon, where, he said, people had other things to worry about.
"I wish we could just tell everyone," said Tomás. "Post the photos and finish it."
"So do I," said Inês. "But if we do that, we could ruin the investigation. And Sergeant Costa said..."
"I know what Sergeant Costa said."

Matilde was at school every day, as perfect and as distant as ever. Twice Inês decided to ask her directly, and twice she changed her mind at the last moment. Because what if Tomás was right? What if the photos had come from Mr Viana himself?
Then, on the last Friday of March, the day before the Easter holidays, Tomás came running across the playground with his new phone in his hand. He was pale.
"Have you seen the group?"

Carlos Mota had posted a photo on Ribeira Alta Unida. It had been taken from a car across the road, a little blurred but clear enough. It showed Inês, Priya, Tomás and Ms Sousa coming out of the GNR post.
Look who's been visiting the GNR. A teacher and three kids, one of them from the Indian family, telling stories about honest local businesses. Ask yourselves who's paying them.
The post had been online for two hours. It had already been shared a hundred and twelve times.
Inês was still staring at it when her own phone buzzed. A message on the WaterWatch chat.
He knows you have something. He's been asking questions at the factory. We need to talk. The bridge, tomorrow, 7 a.m. Come alone.
It was signed with a small bird.

chapters.title: The Girl on the Bridge
paragraphs: The fog was so thick that morning that Inês could hear the river but not see it. She stood in the middle of the bridge with her hands in her pockets, feeling stupid. Come alone, the message had said. She had told nobody, which was probably the most stupid thing of all.
At five past seven, a figure came out of the fog from the other side. A red coat. Long dark hair.
Matilde stopped a metre away and put her hands on the stone railing, as if she needed something to hold on to.
"I'm Kestrel," she said. "But you knew that already, didn't you?"
"I thought so," said Inês. "I wasn't sure."
"Good. That means nobody else is sure either." For the first time since September, Matilde smiled. It didn't last long. "I've got something of yours."
She took a phone out of her pocket. It had a cracked screen and a sticker of a football club on the back. Tomás's phone.

They talked for almost an hour, walking up and down the bridge so that they wouldn't freeze. Afterwards, in the garage, Inês told the others everything, and she tried to tell it exactly as Matilde had told it to her.

"She said she had been watching the lorry from her bedroom window since last spring. Her room's at the top of the house, the one that looks over the service road. She said she had always thought it was normal, a company lorry doing its job, until she noticed that it never came in daylight."
"And the photos?" asked Priya.

"She told me she had found the forms in her father's office one evening when she was waiting for him. She said the numbers didn't make sense, so she sent an email to the treatment plant from the office computer, pretending to be from the factory. That's the email on the card. She said she had taken the photos of Mota from her window with her father's old camera."
Tomás was turning his phone over and over in his hands, as if he couldn't quite believe it was real. "Did she say why she took this?"

"She said she had been hiding behind the wall that night, filming too. When we ran and Mota went back to his lorry, she picked up your phone so that he wouldn't find it. She said she had kept it switched off for weeks because she was scared. Then, before Christmas, she decided to charge it in the office and connect it to the Wi-Fi so the video would reach us."
"And sensor seven?" asked Priya.

"She said she had watched Mota throw it into the river that first night in October. Weeks later, at low tide, she had pulled it out of the mud. The night before the clean-up, she put the card inside and pushed it back into the mud exactly where she knew Tomás would be walking."
"Why didn't she just give it back?"

"She said she couldn't risk being seen with us. She asked me not to tell anyone that she's Kestrel, not yet." Inês hesitated. "And she said she still doesn't know if her father knows about Mota. She said that was the part she was most afraid of finding out."
There was a long silence. Somewhere outside, Avô Zé was arguing with a neighbour about tomatoes.
"So she's not a spoilt rich girl," said Tomás finally.
"And you're not a lazy kid who can only fix bikes," said Priya. "Everybody's wrong about everybody. It's the national sport."

On the Tuesday of the Easter holidays, Priya invited all three of them to lunch. Her grandmother, whom Priya called Ammamma, had arrived from Kochi the week before. She was a small woman with silver glasses who had taught English in a secondary school for thirty-five years and who corrected everybody's grammar, including the TV's.

The flat smelt of coconut and curry leaves. There was fish curry, rice and appam, a soft, round flatbread with a crispy edge, which Tomás ate six of before anyone had sat down. At the table three languages were spoken at the same time: Malayalam between Priya's mother and Ammamma, Portuguese between Priya and her little brother, and English whenever anybody wanted everybody to understand.

"In India English is not a foreign language," Ammamma told them. "It's one of the languages of the government, the courts and the universities. But it's our English. We have our own words." She looked at Priya. "What do we say when a meeting is moved to an earlier time?"
"Prepone," said Priya, rolling her eyes. "It isn't in British dictionaries, Ammamma."
"Then the British dictionaries are missing a very useful word."

Matilde came late, which was not like her. She brought a box of pastéis de nata, sat down nervously at the end of the table and didn't say much at first. But when Ammamma discovered that she was learning to make films with her phone, the two of them talked for half an hour. Ammamma, who had once made a short documentary with her students about the fishermen of Kochi, wanted to know everything: what Matilde filmed, who she showed her films to, why she never put herself in them. Matilde, who usually answered questions with one word, answered every single one.

After lunch, they joined a video call with Thandi and Aroha, who both happened to be at home. Ammamma took over immediately. She and Thandi spent ten minutes arguing about cricket, which is played in all three countries, and which none of the teenagers in Ribeira Alta understood at all. Aroha taught everyone to say kia ora, a Māori greeting, and explained that te reo Māori is one of the official languages of New Zealand.

"India, South Africa and New Zealand are all in the Commonwealth," said Ammamma. "That's why we all play cricket and drink too much tea. It's a long and complicated story. Some parts of it are not very nice."
When the call was over, Priya and Matilde were left alone on the balcony for a moment. Inês, who was carrying plates to the kitchen, heard them through the open door.
"Can I tell you something?" said Matilde. "When you arrived last year, I thought you were the shy Indian girl who's good at maths. That's all. I didn't bother to find out anything else."
"I thought you were the rich girl who never says thank you," said Priya. "We were both a bit right and mostly wrong."
"Which part was right?"
"I've never heard you say thank you."
Matilde laughed. It was the first time Inês had ever heard her laugh properly.
"Ammamma always says the same thing," Priya went on. "When somebody tells you a story about a whole group of people, ask yourself who is telling it, and what they get out of it."
"Carlos Mota," said Matilde quietly.
"Carlos Mota."
At that moment Matilde's phone buzzed. She glanced at the screen, and Inês, standing in the doorway with a pile of plates, saw all the colour leave her face at once.
"It's my father," Matilde said. Her voice had gone very small. She turned the phone round so that they could read it.
I've just seen what's on your laptop. I know about Kestrel. Come home. Now.

chapters.title: The Man Who Shouted Loudest
paragraphs: Matilde called Inês at eleven o'clock that night. She was whispering, and every few sentences she stopped to listen.
The next morning Inês told the others what she had said. She had to tell it twice, because Tomás kept interrupting.

"She said her father had been waiting for her in the kitchen with her laptop open on the table. He asked her why she hadn't come to him. She told him she had been afraid that he was part of it." Inês took a breath. "She said he didn't shout. He just sat there for a long time. Then he told her that he had trusted Carlos Mota for twenty years, that Mota's father had helped the company when times were hard, and that he had paid MotaTrans every single month to take the waste to the plant. He said he had never once checked."
"Do you believe him?" asked Priya.

"Matilde does. She said he looked ill." Inês hesitated. "He's promised to go to the GNR himself, with his lawyer. But he asked her to wait and not to tell anyone until he had spoken to the lawyer. And he made her delete everything from her laptop. He said the lawyer would want the originals."
"So the only copies are ours," said Tomás. "And the GNR's."
Two weeks later, Carlos Mota posted again.

This time there was a photo: a short metal pipe coming out of a wall, pouring bright purple water into a river. Underneath, he had written: This is what the laundry does when nobody is watching. The parish council must act.

Within a day the post had been shared six hundred times. Within a week the parish council had announced a public meeting for Friday the sixth of June, at six o'clock in the sports pavilion, "to discuss the state of the river and the licence of a local business".
Priya didn't cry this time. She opened her laptop.
"Ammamma's question," she said. "Who made this photo, and what do they get out of it? Let's start with the first part."

It took her less than ten minutes. A reverse image search found the same photo on a news website from 2018, in an article about a river in another country, on another continent. Somebody had cut off the bottom of the picture, where the original caption had been, and made the colours a little brighter.
"It's worth checking the laundry too," said Inês. "Just to be sure."

So they cycled down and walked round the back of Rajan's Wash and Dry with Priya's uncle, who looked at the photo on Inês's phone and laughed for the first time in months. The back wall of the laundry was covered in white render. The wall in the photo was made of old yellow bricks. And there was no pipe. There had never been a pipe.
"He didn't even try to make it look like here," said Tomás. "He didn't need to. People believed it because they wanted to."

They decided to do the thing that Dr Fraser had told them to do in December: if you can't prove something, don't say it. So they spent the next three weekends collecting proof. They knocked on doors along the river and wrote down what people told them.

Dona Rosa, who had lived next to the old garage for forty years, said that she had never seen anything come out of the laundry except clean towels and Rajan's terrible music. Senhor Abel told them that he had seen blue lorries on the service road on Thursday nights for more than a year. He said that he had once asked Carlos Mota about them, and that Mota had told him to mind his own business. The woman at the bakery asked them whether they were sure about all this. When Inês said yes, she asked them to put a poster for the meeting in her window.

Not everybody was friendly. One man told them to stop wasting their time on foreigners. Another told them that children should stay out of adult problems, and closed the door before Inês could answer.

Every evening Inês typed up the statements, and Priya saved them in the shared cloud folder with the graphs and the photos from the card. "Remember to put the date on everything," Priya said. "Proof without a date is just gossip."

Meanwhile, Ms Sousa had had an idea. The WaterWatch final was on the sixth of June too, at seven o'clock, which was exactly one hour after the start of the town meeting. She went to see the president of the parish council, Senhor Fonseca, who was a former student of hers and still slightly afraid of her.

"He's agreed," she told them afterwards. "You'll speak at the meeting. Your presentation for the final will be shown live on the big screen in the pavilion, and the jury will be watching from Edinburgh, Cape Town and Wellington. So you'll be presenting to two juries at the same time. One of them speaks English. The other one votes."
"No pressure, then," said Tomás.

For the rest of May they did nothing but work. Priya rebuilt the graphs so that anyone could understand them. Tomás practised the technical part until he could explain a pH reading to his grandfather. Inês wrote the presentation five times and threw away four of them. Matilde, who still wasn't allowed to be seen with them, sent them messages at night: short ones, full of good ideas, signed with the little bird.
Her father hadn't gone to the GNR yet. The lawyer, she said, kept telling him to wait.
"What if he never goes?" asked Priya.
"He'll go," said Matilde. "He has to." But she didn't sound sure.

On Thursday the fifth of June, the night before the meeting, they stayed in the garage until ten, going through the presentation one last time. Avô Zé brought them toasted sandwiches and listened to the whole thing twice, nodding at the parts he understood. When they left, Tomás locked the garage door with the old padlock and hung the key on its nail inside the kitchen, as he always did.
At seven o'clock the next morning, Inês's phone rang. It was Tomás. He was breathing so fast that at first she couldn't understand him.
"Someone's broken into the garage," he said. "The padlock's been cut. They've taken everything. The laptops, the sensors, the box with the memory card. Everything."
"Priya's got backups. She always has backups."

"Priya's on her way here. She's already checked." Tomás's voice cracked. "Whoever took her laptop used it to get into our accounts. The WaterWatch data has been deleted. The cloud folder is empty. The graphs, the photos from the card, all the statements from the neighbours. It's all gone, Inês."
She stood in the middle of her bedroom, still in her pyjamas, holding the phone so tightly that her fingers hurt.
The meeting was in eleven hours. And they had nothing left to show.

chapters.title: Clear Water
paragraphs: The GNR came at eight, looked at the cut padlock, took photographs and wrote everything down. Priya sat on the floor of the empty garage with her back against the wall and said nothing at all, which frightened Inês more than anything else that morning.
At twenty past seven a message had arrived on Priya's phone. She hadn't even looked at it. It was Inês who finally picked the phone up and read it out loud.

It was from Aroha. It was twenty past six in the evening in Wellington, and she said that she had just noticed that Ribeira Alta's dashboard was empty. She asked whether something had gone wrong. Then she said that it didn't matter anyway, because her team had been downloading the data of all three schools every night since October, to make their comparison graphs. She said she would send everything in five minutes.
Priya looked up. "Every night?"
"Every night since October."
"Kia ora, Aroha," said Priya, and burst into tears for the first time all year.

After that, things started to happen quickly. Thandi wrote to say that her team still had the graphs Priya had shown in the December and March calls, and sent them before anyone had asked. Tomás suddenly hit his own forehead with his hand.

"My old phone," he said. "The one Matilde gave back. My mum had already bought me a new one, so I put it in my drawer. I never even switched it on." He was already running for his bike. "The video's still on it. The original."

Inês made a list of the neighbours who had talked to them and started making phone calls. If their statements had been deleted, then people would have to say it themselves. Dona Rosa said that she would be there in her best dress. Senhor Abel said he would come if somebody gave him a lift.

At half past ten Matilde called. Her father had gone to the GNR at eight o'clock that morning, she said, as soon as he had heard about the break-in. He had taken every invoice and every bank payment to MotaTrans for the last five years. She said that he had finally stopped listening to his lawyer.

By six o'clock the sports pavilion was full. There were people on the benches, people standing along the walls, and children sitting on the floor in front of the big screen. Inês's parents were there, and Tomás's mother, and Priya's whole family, with Ammamma in the front row holding her handbag on her knees like a weapon. Ms Sousa stood at the side, checking the connection every two minutes.

Carlos Mota spoke first. He was good at it. He was loud and confident, and he said "our river" and "our town" a lot. He showed the photo of the purple pipe on the big screen, and several people nodded.
Then Senhor Fonseca called the students to the front.

They spoke in English, because that was the rule of the final, and Tomás translated each part into Portuguese for the room. Inês began with the photo of the purple pipe. Next to it, Priya put the page from the 2018 news website, the one with the original caption, in a different country, on a different continent. A long murmur went round the pavilion.

Then the graphs, which Aroha's team had saved: the same pattern again and again, a sudden spike in the middle of every Thursday night, at the old pier, nowhere near the laundry. Then the lab report from the University of Porto, which had found industrial dyes in the mud and nothing unusual near Rajan's Wash and Dry. Then Dona Rosa, who stood up in her best dress and said, very clearly, that she had lived next to that garage for forty years and had never seen anything come out of it but clean towels. Senhor Abel told everybody what he had seen on the service road, and what Carlos Mota had told him when he asked.
Last of all, the video.

Priya froze it on the one second when the torch lit up the back of the lorry. The number plate filled the screen. Somebody near the door read it out loud, and then somebody else said, "That's the lorry parked outside."

Carlos Mota was on his feet. He was shouting that it was all lies, that the video could have been made anywhere, that these children were being used by people who wanted to destroy an honest local business.
"I agree that an honest local business has been destroyed," said a voice at the back.

It was Mr Viana. He walked slowly to the front. He told the room that he had paid MotaTrans for years to take the waste from his factory to a treatment plant, and that the plant had received nothing. He said he had given all the documents to the GNR that morning. Then he turned to Priya's uncle, who was sitting very still in the third row.
"Senhor Rajan," he said, "I should have checked. If I had checked, none of this would have happened to you. I'm sorry."

The last person to speak was a short woman with tired eyes, who had been standing by the wall in plain clothes all evening. Sergeant Costa said that an investigation had been opened in March, that the offices and lorries of MotaTrans had been searched that afternoon, and that two laptops, several homemade sensors and a box containing a memory card had been found in the cab of one of them. She asked Senhor Mota to come with her. Two officers were already waiting at the door.
For a moment nobody moved. Then Matilde stood up in the middle of the benches, in her red coat.
"There's one more thing," she said. "The photos on the memory card were taken by me. I'm Kestrel."
The applause started at the back and went all the way to the front, and it went on for a long time.

At seven o'clock the WaterWatch jury announced the results. Cape Town won, for the sewage pipe they had got repaired. Ribeira Alta received the jury's special prize. Dr Fraser leaned towards his camera. "In December I asked you to explain your graphs," he said. "You've done more than that. You've proved them."

By the end of June, MotaTrans had closed, and Carlos Mota had been told that he would have to explain himself in court. The hotel that had left came back to Rajan's Wash and Dry, and Dona Rosa brought a cake every Saturday for a month. Some of the people who had shared Mota's posts apologised. Most of them simply stopped mentioning it, as if it had never happened. Avô Zé said that was normal. He said he had been waiting thirty-seven years to see that lorry stopped, and that he didn't need anybody to say sorry.

On the last day of school the four of them cycled to the bridge. They stood in a row with their bikes, looking down at the water. On Priya's phone, the sensors showed nothing strange at all. Every Thursday night for a month had been quiet.
"This time next year," said Matilde, "I'll be doing whatever I've decided."
"What have you decided?" asked Tomás.
"I haven't decided yet. That's the point."
Inês leaned over the railing. The river was still brown, still slow, the colour of cold tea. She still couldn't see the bottom.

"Not yet," she said, mostly to herself. Below her, the water moved on towards the sea, carrying the light in small, bright ripples, and for the first time in her life she was happy just to watch it go.

reading.title: Sensor Number Seven
text: On the first day of school, Inês Pacheco stopped on the old bridge in Ribeira Alta and looked down at the river. It was brown and slow, the colour of cold tea. She had been crossing that bridge every school day since she was six, and she had never seen the bottom.

Her English teacher, Ms Sousa, had been planning something all summer. This year the school was taking part in WaterWatch, an international project with partner schools in Cape Town, in South Africa, and Wellington, in New Zealand. Each school had to build cheap sensors, put them in a local river and share the data online. Everything would be in English, because it was the language all the students shared. "By June," said Ms Sousa, "you will have collected more information about this river than anyone in this town."

Inês formed a team with her best friend Tomás, who could fix almost anything, and Priya Nair, a quiet girl who had arrived from Kochi, in India, the year before. "I've been teaching myself to code for two years," Priya said. Then the teacher added a fourth member: Matilde Viana, whose father owned the town's dye works.

At a careers session, the students wrote about their future. "This time in ten years, I'll be working as an environmental engineer," Inês wrote. Matilde's paper was blank. "I'll be doing whatever my father has already decided," she said.
During their first video call, the team discovered that English is not the same everywhere. In South Africa, "just now" can mean "later", and in New Zealand everything good is "sweet as".

The team built seven sensors in the garage of Tomás's grandfather, Avô Zé, who had worked at the dye works for thirty-one years. In October they put the sensors in the river. Sensor seven was tied to the old pier, a few metres from a wide concrete pipe.

For a week, nothing happened. Then, at 3.20 one Friday morning, Priya sent Inês a message. At 3.02 the temperature next to the pier had jumped by nine degrees, and the water had suddenly become very cloudy. At 3.19 sensor seven had stopped working. "Sensors don't switch themselves off," Priya wrote. "Somebody has switched it off."

reading.title: Kestrel
text: The next morning, Inês, Tomás and Priya went to the pier before school. The wooden post was still there, but somebody had cut the rope, and sensor seven had gone. The stones around the big concrete pipe were stained purple, and the mud smelt of chemicals. Near an old drain on the service road there were wide tyre marks. A heavy lorry had been there.
At lunch, Matilde sat with them for the first time. When Priya showed her the graph, she got angry. "My father's factory has been inspected every year," she said, and left.

Tomás's grandfather, Avô Zé, told them a story. One night in 1989, during his night shift, he had seen a lorry next to the same drain. Some men had connected a hose and were emptying something into it. The next morning the river was black. He had told his boss, but the boss had said that he had dreamt it. "That drain goes straight into the big pipe by the pier," he said.

The friends didn't give up. Tomás came up with a smaller sensor that could be hidden inside a plastic bottle, Priya set up a backup system, and Inês found out that the service road had been closed to traffic for years. By the end of October, a new hidden sensor was in the water.

In November, a strange message arrived on the WaterWatch platform. The sender called themselves Kestrel and had no school, no country and no photo. "Watch the drain on the service road," the message said. "Thursday nights, after 2 a.m. Don't go alone."

On Thursday night, the three friends hid behind an old boat near the pier. At 2.52 a tanker lorry with no name on its side came down the road. A big man pushed a hose into the drain and started emptying the tanker. Tomás was filming with his phone, but the screen was too bright. Suddenly a torch beam stopped on Inês's face. "Hey!" shouted the man. "Who's there?"

fichas.title: The Phone in the Mud
fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 3 · Grammar: future continuous and future perfect, present perfect continuous, phrasal verbs

reading.title: The Phone in the Mud
text: They ran. Tomás slipped on the wet stones, and his phone flew out of his hand and landed in the mud. There was no time to pick it up. When the man got close, Priya turned round and switched on her phone's flash. For one second he couldn't see, and that second was enough. The three friends escaped through a vineyard and didn't stop until they reached the bus shelter by the church.

The next day, Priya checked the data. The hidden sensor had recorded the same pattern as in October. "But numbers aren't a lorry," she said. "Anyone can say our sensor's broken." Tomás's video was the real proof, and it was lost. Then Priya had an idea. If the phone was still on and somebody took it somewhere with Wi-Fi, the video would upload automatically. "By tonight the battery will have died," said Inês. "Probably," Priya answered. "But probably isn't certainly."
Nothing arrived for weeks. When they went back to the pier in daylight, the phone had gone, and somebody had raked the mud flat. Priya wrote to Kestrel, but Kestrel never answered.

In December, the WaterWatch teams had their last video call of the term. The teams from Cape Town and Wellington had photos, letters and plans. Ribeira Alta only had a graph. "In June you won't just be showing us graphs," said Dr Fraser, the coordinator. "You'll be explaining them. And if you can't prove something, don't say it."

On the evening of the twenty-third of December, Inês was at her grandmother's flat in Porto when Priya sent her twelve messages. The video had uploaded at 11.58 p.m., from a Wi-Fi network called VIANA-OFFICE: the dye works.

Inês watched the video in the bathroom. It showed the lorry, the hose and a number plate for less than a second. Then the phone fell into the mud and kept recording. After a minute, someone walked into the picture and picked it up. The screen lit up her face: a girl in a red coat, with long dark hair.
It was Matilde.

reading.title: The Red Coat
text: On the first day of the second term, Inês found Matilde alone in the library and showed her the video. Matilde's face didn't change. "Delete that," she said. "If you'd stayed at home that night, none of this would have happened. If Tomás hadn't been filming, that man wouldn't have seen you." Then she said, "Stay away from the river," and walked out.

That week, in Citizenship, Mr Lobo asked the class to look at the labels inside their clothes. Tomás's hoodie had been made in Bangladesh, designed in Sweden and sold in a shopping centre in Matosinhos. Mr Lobo explained that a lot of clothes are only worn a few times and then thrown away, and that dyeing cloth uses enormous amounts of water and chemicals. "In a good factory, the water is cleaned before it's returned to the river," he said. "In a bad one, it isn't."

At break, Tomás looked sadly at his new trainers. "I wish I hadn't bought these," he said. "If I'd known all this, I would have bought the other ones." Priya told him that the other ones were made in the same factory. "If only you'd told me that in August," he sighed.

On the third Saturday of January, hundreds of dead fish were found along the river. Samples of water were collected by the environmental authorities. Priya's data showed another spike on a Thursday night, at 3.06 a.m.

By lunchtime, Carlos Mota, who owned a waste transport company, had posted a message on a local Facebook group. He suggested that the new laundry was poisoning the river. He didn't write a name, but everyone knew it was Rajan's Wash and Dry, which belonged to Priya's uncle. The post was shared more than three hundred times. "Nobody's looking," said Priya. "They've already decided."

The next morning, at seven o'clock, Priya called Inês and asked her to come to the laundry. The front window had been smashed with a stone, and someone had sprayed three words on the door in red paint: GO BACK HOME.

reading.title: Volunteers
text: After the attack on the laundry, Priya didn't come to school for two days. That week, Ms Sousa gave the class Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which was adopted by the United Nations in 1948: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights." The students gave examples of dignity. Then Priya spoke. "Here I'm always the Indian girl," she said. "Sometimes I would like to be Priya."

Inês decided they needed to do something people could see. Organising it took three weeks. Inês wrote to the parish council, Tomás talked to the scouts, and Priya designed posters in Portuguese and in English, so that students from Brazil, Ukraine and Nepal knew they were invited too. On the last Saturday of February, the town would clean the riverbank. Afterwards, everyone would have a free coffee at Rajan's laundry, where the new window was being put in that same morning.

By Friday, almost everything had been arranged. Gloves and bags would be provided by the parish council, and the rubbish would be collected by the scouts' van. Water samples were going to be taken by a biology lecturer from the University of Porto. Posters had been put up all over town.

On Saturday it rained. Although Inês was sure nobody would come, more than a hundred people turned up, including Avô Zé and his old friends from the dye works. Matilde came too. She worked for three hours without speaking to anyone. People stared at her, but she didn't seem to notice.

By lunchtime, more than two hundred bags of rubbish had been collected. Most of it was plastic, but there were also a lot of clothes. "These samples will be analysed in our lab next week," the lecturer promised.

Near the pier, Tomás's boot sank into the mud. He pulled out something hard: sensor seven. It had been lying in the river for months. However, its cap was clean. Inside there was a memory card in a dry, new plastic bag. Somebody had put it there for them to find. On the bag, someone had drawn a small bird with its wings spread.

reading.title: What the Card Remembered
text: They opened the memory card in Priya's kitchen. There were forty-three photos on it. Most of them showed waste transport forms. Every Thursday, for more than a year, the Viana dye works had paid a company called MotaTrans to collect twenty thousand litres of dye waste. The waste was supposed to be taken to a treatment plant near Porto. Every form had been signed by C. Mota.

Another photo showed an email from the treatment plant. It said that no deliveries from MotaTrans had been received there since the previous March. "So the factory pays him," said Inês slowly, "but he empties the waste into the drain and keeps the money." "And then he tells the town that my uncle is poisoning the river," said Priya, "so that nobody looks at him."

The last photos had been taken at night, from a window above the service road. In one of them, the light in the lorry's cab was on, and the driver's face was perfectly clear. It was Carlos Mota. When Avô Zé saw it, he said that the company had belonged to Mota's father in the past. "I never saw the driver's face in 1989," he said. "I've always wished I had gone closer."
But who had taken the photos? Inês was sure it was Matilde. Tomás wasn't. "Maybe it was her father," he said. "If he knew about Mota, sending us after him would make him look innocent."

Two weeks later, the university's results arrived. Traces of industrial dyes had been found in the mud near the pier, but the water near the laundry was no worse than anywhere else. Their friends abroad gave them advice. "Take it to the people whose job it is," said Thandi. "If we'd posted our photos online," said Aroha, "the farmer would have cleaned everything up."

So they went to the GNR with Ms Sousa. Sergeant Costa made copies of everything. "This will be investigated," she said, "but you mustn't tell anybody." Weeks passed, and nothing happened. Then, on the last Friday of March, Carlos Mota posted a photo of them leaving the GNR post: "Ask yourselves who's paying them." A few minutes later, Kestrel wrote: "He knows you have something. The bridge, tomorrow, 7 a.m. Come alone."

reading.title: The Girl on the Bridge
text: At seven in the morning, Inês waited on the bridge in thick fog. A girl in a red coat came out of the fog. "I'm Kestrel," Matilde said. "But you knew that already, didn't you?" Then she took Tomás's phone out of her pocket and gave it back.

Later, in the garage, Inês told the others everything. "She said she had been watching the lorry from her bedroom window since last spring," she explained. "She told me she had found the forms in her father's office and had sent an email to the treatment plant." Matilde had picked up Tomás's phone at the pier so that Mota wouldn't find it, and before Christmas she had charged it in the office so the video would upload. She said she couldn't risk being seen with them. And she still didn't know if her father knew about Mota.

During the Easter holidays, Priya invited everyone to lunch. Her grandmother, Ammamma, who had taught English in Kochi for thirty-five years, was visiting. Three languages were spoken at the table: Malayalam, Portuguese and English. "In India English is not a foreign language," Ammamma said. "It's one of the languages of the government, the courts and the universities. But it's our English. We have our own words."

After lunch they had a video call with Thandi and Aroha. Ammamma and Thandi argued happily about cricket, and Aroha taught everyone to say kia ora, a Māori greeting. "India, South Africa and New Zealand are all in the Commonwealth," Ammamma explained. "It's a long and complicated story."

Later, on the balcony, Matilde told Priya that she had always thought Priya was just "the shy Indian girl who's good at maths". Priya answered that she had thought Matilde was "the rich girl who never says thank you". "We were both a bit right and mostly wrong," she said. She told Matilde what her grandmother always said: when somebody tells you a story about a whole group of people, ask who is telling it, and what they get out of it.
At that moment Matilde's phone buzzed. The message, which was from her father, made her face go white. I've just seen what's on your laptop. I know about Kestrel. Come home. Now.

reading.title: The Man Who Shouted Loudest
text: Matilde called Inês late that night, and the next morning Inês told the others what had happened. Mr Viana had been waiting for his daughter in the kitchen, with her laptop open. He asked her why she hadn't come to him. She told him that she had been afraid he was part of it. He said that he had trusted Carlos Mota for twenty years and had paid MotaTrans every month. He promised to go to the GNR with his lawyer, but he asked Matilde not to tell anyone until then.

Two weeks later, Mota posted a photo of a metal pipe pouring purple water into a river. "This is what the laundry does when nobody is watching," he wrote. Soon the parish council announced a public meeting for the sixth of June.

Priya decided to check the photo. A reverse image search found the same picture on a news website from 2018, in an article about a river in another country. Then they went to look at the back of the laundry. The wall was white, not yellow, and there was no pipe. "People believed it because they wanted to," said Tomás.

The friends spent three weekends interviewing neighbours. Dona Rosa said that she had never seen anything come out of the laundry except clean towels. Senhor Abel told them that he had seen blue lorries on the service road on Thursday nights, and that Mota had once told him to mind his own business. Not everyone was friendly. One man told them to stop wasting their time on foreigners.

Ms Sousa managed to convince the president of the parish council to let the students speak at the meeting. Their WaterWatch final would be shown live on a big screen in the pavilion. "You'll be presenting to two juries at the same time," she said.

On the night before the meeting, someone broke into Avô Zé's garage. The laptops, the sensors and the memory card were taken. Whoever had Priya's laptop used it to delete the WaterWatch data and empty their cloud folder. The meeting was in eleven hours, and they had nothing left to show.

fichas.title: Clear Water
fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 9 · Grammar: defining and non-defining relative clauses, gerund and infinitive, reported speech

reading.title: Clear Water
text: The morning after the break-in, a message arrived from Aroha in Wellington, where it was already evening. She said that her team had been downloading the data of all three schools every night since October. Thandi, who still had their graphs, sent them too. Then Tomás remembered his old phone, which was in a drawer at home. The original video was still on it.
At half past ten Matilde called. Her father had gone to the GNR that morning with every invoice and every payment to MotaTrans.

By six o'clock the sports pavilion was full. Carlos Mota, who spoke first, was loud and confident, and he showed his photo of the purple pipe again. Then the students presented their work in English, while Tomás translated it into Portuguese. They showed the 2018 website where the photo really came from, the graphs with a spike every Thursday night and the report from the university. Dona Rosa and Senhor Abel told everyone what they had seen. Last of all came the video. When the number plate appeared on the screen, someone near the door said, "That's the lorry parked outside."

Mota started shouting that it was all lies. Then Mr Viana walked to the front. He told the room that he had paid MotaTrans for years and that the treatment plant had received nothing. He turned to Priya's uncle. "If I had checked, none of this would have happened to you," he said. "I'm sorry."

Finally, Sergeant Costa explained that an investigation had been opened in March. That afternoon, the laptops, the sensors and the memory card had been found in one of Mota's lorries. She asked him to come with her. Then Matilde stood up. "The photos on the memory card were taken by me," she said. "I'm Kestrel."

Cape Town won the WaterWatch final, and Ribeira Alta received the jury's special prize. By the end of June MotaTrans had closed, and the hotel which had left came back to Rajan's laundry. On the last day of school, the four friends stood on the bridge. The river was still brown, but on Thursday nights it was quiet now.
