sebenta.title: Review: present and past tenses
sebenta.html:
Present Simple

FormUseExamples
I/you/we/they work
he/she/it works
neg.: don't / doesn't + verb
quest.: Do / Does + subject + verb?		 • habits and routines
• permanent situations, facts
• timetables
• with adverbs of frequency		 She works in a hospital.
Water boils at 100 °C.
The bus leaves at 8.15.
I usually walk to school.

Adverbs of frequency (always · usually · often · sometimes · rarely · hardly ever · never) go before the main verb but after be: He never complains. / He is never late. Spelling: watch → watches, study → studies, go → goes, have → has.

Present Continuous

FormUseExamples
am / is / are + verb-ing • actions happening now
• temporary situations
• changing situations
• fixed future arrangements		 She's talking to the teacher.
I'm staying with my aunt this week.
The climate is getting warmer.
We're meeting at 6 tomorrow.
Stative verbs are not normally used in continuous tenses: know, believe, understand, want, need, like, love, hate, prefer, belong, own, seem, mean. I need help (not I'm needing).

Past Simple

FormUseExamples
regular: verb + -ed
irregular: 2nd column (p. 14)
neg.: didn't + verb
quest.: Did + subject + verb?		 • finished actions at a definite time in the past
• a sequence of past events
• past habits (also used to)		 We visited London last year.
She opened the door and went in.
I used to play the piano.

Time markers: yesterday · last week/year · two days ago · in 2015 · when I was a child.

Past Continuous

FormUseExamples
was / were + verb-ing • action in progress at a past moment
• background to a shorter action (past simple)
• two parallel actions		 At 8 pm I was doing my homework.
I was walking home when it started to rain.
While I was cooking, he was reading.
Past Simple vs Past Continuous: when + past simple interrupts; while / as + past continuous gives the background. The phone rang while I was sleeping.

sebenta.title: Review: present perfect · future · overview
sebenta.html:
Present Perfect Simple

FormUseExamples
have / has + past participle (3rd column, p. 14)
neg.: haven't / hasn't
quest.: Have / Has + subject + p.p.?		 • unfinished past (started in the past, continues now) → for / since
• life experience → ever, never, before
• recent news / results evident now → just, already, yet		 I've lived here for ten years / since 2016.
Have you ever been to Ireland?
She has just arrived. · I've already finished; he hasn't started yet.
Past Simple vs Present Perfect: finished time (yesterday, in 2010, ago, last…) → past simple; time up to now (today, this year, ever, since, so far) → present perfect. I saw him yesterday. / I have seen him today. Note: been = went and came back; gone = not back yet.

The future

FormUseExamples
Will
will + verb		• spontaneous decisions, offers, promises
• predictions based on opinion (I think, probably)		I'll help you with that.
I think robots will do most jobs.
Going to
am/is/are going to + verb		• plans and intentions
• predictions based on evidence		I'm going to study engineering.
Look at the sky – it's going to rain.
Present Continuousfixed future arrangements (time and place decided)We're flying to Dublin on Friday.
Present Simpletimetables, programmesThe exam starts at 9.
After when, as soon as, until, before, after, if use the present, not will: I'll call you when I arrive.

Overview of tenses

TenseForm (verb work)Typical markers
Present Simplework / worksalways, usually, every day, on Mondays
Present Continuousam/is/are workingnow, at the moment, today, this week, Look!
Past Simpleworkedyesterday, ago, last…, in 2010, when
Past Continuouswas/were workingwhile, as, at 8 o'clock yesterday
Present Perfecthave/has workedfor, since, ever, never, just, already, yet, so far
Present Perfect Cont.have/has been workingfor, since, all day, how long, lately
Past Perfecthad workedby the time, before, after, already, when
Future (will)will worktomorrow, next…, soon, I think, probably
Going toam/is/are going to workplans, intentions, evidence
Future Continuouswill be workingthis time tomorrow, at 10 tomorrow
Future Perfectwill have workedby then, by 2030, by the time

sebenta.title: Present perfect continuous · Past perfect
sebenta.html:
Present Perfect Continuous

FormUseExamples
have / has been + verb-ing
neg.: haven't / hasn't been + -ing
quest.: Have / Has + subject + been + -ing?		 • unfinished activity, emphasis on duration (how long?)
• repeated actions up to now
• an activity that has just stopped, with results we can see now		 I've been studying for three hours.
She's been calling you all morning.
You look tired – have you been running?

Markers: for · since · how long · all day / all week · lately · recently · the whole afternoon.

Simple vs Continuous: simple = result / how many (I've written three emails); continuous = activity / how long (I've been writing emails all day). Stative verbs → simple only (I've known him for years).

Past Perfect Simple

FormUseExamples
had + past participle (all persons)
neg.: hadn't + p.p.
quest.: Had + subject + p.p.?		 • an action completed before another past action or moment ("the past of the past")
• with by the time, after, before, when, already, never … before
• in reported speech and the 3rd conditional		 When I arrived, the film had already started.
She had never flown before that day.
By 2020 they had moved twice.
He said he had lost his keys.
SequenceExample
1st action → past perfect
2nd action → past simple		The train had left (1st) when we got to the station (2nd).
After she had finished her homework, she went out.
same order, with and then / after thatShe finished her homework and then went out. (two past simples)
Past Perfect Continuous (had been + -ing) stresses the duration of an activity up to a past moment: He had been waiting for an hour when the bus came. · Her eyes were red – she had been crying.

For, since and ago

WordUseExamples
for+ a period of time; with present perfect (simple / continuous), past perfect and past simpleI've been here for two hours. · They lived in Rome for a year.
since+ the starting point; with perfect tenses onlyShe's worked here since 2019 / since she left school.
agoafter a period of time; with the past simple onlyThey moved here three years ago. (not have moved … ago)

Tenses together

I have known Ana since we were at school. · It has been raining since I got up. · By the time the firefighters arrived, the forest had been burning for hours. · How long have you been learning English? (duration) / When did you start? (moment)

sebenta.title: Future continuous · Future perfect
sebenta.html:
Future Continuous

FormUseExamples
will be + verb-ing
neg.: won't be + -ing
quest.: Will + subject + be + -ing?		 • an action in progress at a specific moment in the future
• something that will happen as part of the normal course of events
• polite questions about plans		 This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Rome.
At 9 o'clock we'll be having our English lesson.
I'll be seeing Tom later, so I can tell him.
Will you be using the car tonight?

Markers: this time tomorrow / next week · at 10 o'clock tomorrow · in a year's time · all day tomorrow.

Future Perfect

FormUseExamples
will have + past participle
neg.: won't have + p.p.
quest.: Will + subject + have + p.p.?		 • an action that will be completed before a moment in the future
• usually with by + time, by the time, by then, in … years' time		 By June I'll have finished the course.
By the time you arrive, we'll have eaten.
In 2050 scientists will have found a cure.
She won't have left by then.
Future Perfect Continuous (will have been + -ing) stresses the duration up to a future moment: By next month I'll have been working here for a year.
Continuous vs Perfect: At 8 pm I'll be doing my homework (in progress at that moment) ≠ By 8 pm I'll have done my homework (finished before that moment). Remember: after by the time, when, as soon as use the present simple, not will.

Overview of future forms

FormStructureMain use
Willwill + verbdecisions made now, offers, promises, predictions (opinion), facts
Going toam/is/are going to + verbplans, intentions; predictions with evidence
Present Continuousam/is/are + -ingfixed arrangements (time and place decided)
Present Simpleverb / verb-stimetables; after when, if, as soon as, until
Future Continuouswill be + -ingaction in progress at a future moment
Future Perfectwill have + p.p.action completed before a future moment (by)
Future Perfect Cont.will have been + -ingduration up to a future moment

Predicting the future of work, science and the planet

  • Degrees of certainty: will definitely / certainly · will probably · may / might / could + verb · probably won't · definitely won't. Electric cars will probably replace petrol cars. · We might live on Mars one day.
  • Useful verbs: be likely / unlikely to, expect, predict, be bound to. Sea levels are likely to rise. · Experts predict that AI will create new jobs.

sebenta.title: Conditionals · Wish and if only
sebenta.html:
TypeFormUseExample
ZeroIf + present simple,
present simple		facts, general truths, things that always happenIf you heat ice, it melts.
If I'm tired, I go to bed early.
FirstIf + present simple,
will + verb		real possibility in the present or futureIf it rains, we'll stay at home.
If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.
SecondIf + past simple,
would + verb		unreal, hypothetical or unlikely present / future situations; adviceIf I had more time, I would volunteer.
If I were you, I'd apologise.
Third ★ newIf + past perfect,
would have + past participle		hypothetical past (it did not happen); regrets, criticismIf I had studied, I would have passed.
If you'd told me, I could have helped.
If they hadn't cut down the trees, the river wouldn't have flooded.

Notes

  • The if-clause can come first or second. With the if-clause first, use a comma: If I see her, I'll tell her. / I'll tell her if I see her.
  • Other modals can replace will / would: can, may, might, could, should. If you finish early, you can leave. · If I'd known, I might have come.
  • In the second conditional, were is used for all persons in formal English: If she were here…
  • Alternatives to if: unless (= if not), as long as / provided that (= only if), in case (as a precaution). I won't go unless you come too. · Take a coat in case it gets cold.
  • Third conditional contractions: I'd = I had (if-clause) / I would (main clause): If I'd known, I'd have called.
Typical mistakes: If I will see him → If I see him… · If I would have known → If I had known… · If I would be you → If I were you…

Wish and if only

StructureMeaningExamples
wish / if only + past simplea present situation we would like to be differentI wish I had more free time.
If only I were taller. · I wish I could drive.
wish / if only + past perfectregret about the past (it cannot be changed)I wish I hadn't said that.
If only we had left earlier.
wish / if only + would + verbcomplaint or annoyance about someone else's behaviour or a situationI wish you would stop shouting.
If only it would stop raining.
If only is more emphatic than I wish. Hope is used for real possibilities and takes a present / future form: I hope you pass (not I wish you pass). Compare: I wish I had a car (now) / I wish I had bought that car (past).

sebenta.title: The passive voice in all tenses
sebenta.html:
Form: be (in the right tense) + past participle. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject. The agent is introduced by by and is omitted when it is unknown, obvious or unimportant. We use the passive to focus on the action or the result, in formal, scientific and news writing.

Active: Volunteers collect the rubbish every Saturday. → Passive: The rubbish is collected every Saturday (by volunteers).

TenseActivePassive
Present SimpleThey recycle the paper.The paper is recycled.
Present ContinuousThey are recycling the paper.The paper is being recycled.
Past SimpleThey recycled the paper.The paper was recycled.
Past ContinuousThey were recycling the paper.The paper was being recycled.
Present PerfectThey have recycled the paper.The paper has been recycled.
Past PerfectThey had recycled the paper.The paper had been recycled.
Future (will)They will recycle the paper.The paper will be recycled.
Going toThey are going to recycle the paper.The paper is going to be recycled.
Future PerfectThey will have recycled the paper.The paper will have been recycled.
Modal verbsThey must / should / can recycle the paper.The paper must / should / can be recycled.
Modal perfectThey should have recycled the paper.The paper should have been recycled.
  • Questions and negatives follow the verb be: Was the letter sent? · When was the bridge built? · It wasn't delivered.
  • Two objects (give, send, offer, show, tell, pay, teach…): two passives are possible; the person is usually the subject. They gave her a prize. → She was given a prize. / A prize was given to her.
  • Verbs with prepositions keep them: The children were looked after by their aunt.
  • Pronouns change: I → me, he → him, they → them: She helped me. → I was helped by her.
  • Get + past participle is informal: He got fired. · My bike got stolen.
When to use the passive: the agent is unknown (My phone was stolen.), obvious (The thief was arrested.) or less important than the action (Penicillin was discovered in 1928.). Mention the agent with by only when it is new or important information: The telephone was invented by Bell.

Useful passive expressions

ExpressionExamples
be born (always passive)I was born in 2011. · Where were you born?
be made of / from · be made inThis bag is made of recycled plastic. · It was made in Portugal.
be known as / forLisbon is known for its light. · He is known as "the Professor".
It is said / believed / thought that…It is said that the castle is haunted.
be + past participle in news and scienceTwo people were injured in the crash. · The vaccine was tested on 3,000 volunteers.
Step by step: ① find the object → new subject · ② keep the tense of the active verb in be · ③ add the past participle · ④ add by + agent if needed. Someone has broken the window. → The window has been broken.

sebenta.title: Reported speech
sebenta.html:
With a past reporting verb (said, told, asked), tenses, pronouns and time / place expressions move "one step back".

Direct speechReported speech
present simplepast simple
present continuouspast continuous
past simplepast perfect
present perfectpast perfect
past perfectpast perfect (no change)
will / can / maywould / could / might
mustmust / had to
would, could, might, shouldno change
DirectReported
nowthen / at that moment
today / tonightthat day / that night
yesterdaythe day before / the previous day
tomorrowthe next day / the following day
last week / agothe week before / before
next weekthe following week
here · this / thesethere · that / those
I / we / myhe, she, they / his, her, their

Statements

said (that) + clause · told + person + (that) + clause. "I'm leaving tomorrow," she said. → She said (that) she was leaving the next day. · "We have finished," they told me. → They told me they had finished.

No change when the reporting verb is in the present (He says he's busy) or when the statement is still true / a general truth (She said the Earth is round).

Questions

  • Wh- questions: asked / wanted to know / wondered + wh-word + subject + verb (normal word order, no do / does / did, no question mark). "Where do you live?" → He asked me where I lived. · "What time did the train leave?" → She wanted to know what time the train had left.
  • Yes / No questions: asked + if / whether + subject + verb. "Are you tired?" → She asked if I was tired. · "Can you help me?" → He asked whether I could help him.

Commands, requests and advice

PatternExamples
told / ordered + person + to + infinitive
negative: + not to + infinitive		"Sit down." → The teacher told us to sit down.
"Don't touch it!" → She told him not to touch it.
asked + person + to + infinitive (requests)"Could you open the window, please?" → He asked me to open the window.
advised / warned / reminded + person + to + infinitive"You should see a doctor." → She advised me to see a doctor.
suggested + -ing / that + clause"Let's go out." → He suggested going out.
say vs tell: tell needs a person object (He told me that…); say does not (He said (to me) that…). He said me · He told that.

sebenta.title: Relative clauses
sebenta.html:
PronounRefers toExamples
whopeople (subject / object)the scientist who discovered penicillin
whichthings, animals, ideasthe app which I use every day
thatpeople or things (defining clauses only)the job that I applied for
whosepossession (people, things)the girl whose phone was stolen
whompeople, object, formal; after prepositionsthe person to whom I spoke
whereplaces (= in / at which)the town where I was born
whentime (= on / in which)the day when we met
whyreason (the reason why)the reason why he left

Defining relative clauses

Give essential information to identify the noun: without the clause, we do not know who or what we are talking about. No commas. That can replace who / which. The volunteers who clean the beach are students. · This is the film that won the prize.

The pronoun can be omitted when it is the object of the clause: The film (which) we saw was great. · The woman (who) you met is my aunt. It cannot be omitted when it is the subject: The woman who called is my aunt. Test: is there a subject after the pronoun? (we saw, you met) → object → can be omitted.

Non-defining relative clauses

Add extra information about a noun already identified; without the clause, the sentence still makes sense. Between commas. That is not used and the pronoun cannot be omitted. My brother, who lives in Faro, is a doctor. · Sintra, which is near Lisbon, is beautiful. · Malala, whose story is famous, won the Nobel Prize.

Which can refer to the whole previous clause: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.

DefiningNon-defining
Commasnoyes
thatyes (= who / which)no
Omit the object pronounyesno
Meaningidentifies the noun (essential)adds extra information
ExampleThe students who study hard will pass. (only those)The students, who study hard, will pass. (all of them)

Prepositions usually go at the end: the house (which) I grew up in; formal: the house in which I grew up. Do not repeat the object: the book which I read it → the book which I read.

Who's = who is / who has; whose = possession. the boy who's talking (who is) / the boy whose bag is red. Compare who (people) and which (things): the people which → the people who.

sebenta.title: Gerund and infinitive
sebenta.html:
The gerund is the -ing form used as a noun (reading, swimming). The infinitive is to + verb (to read) or the bare infinitive (read) after modals and some verbs.

We use the gerund (-ing)

ContextExamples
as the subject of a sentenceRecycling is important. · Learning languages opens doors.
after prepositions (in, at, of, for, about, without, before, after)She's good at drawing. · He left without saying goodbye. · I'm interested in working abroad.
after certain verbs: enjoy, like, love, hate, mind, finish, stop, avoid, suggest, keep (on), miss, practise, consider, imagine, admit, deny, give up, can't stand, can't help, feel like, look forward toI enjoy playing football. · Would you mind opening the window? · He gave up smoking. · I'm looking forward to seeing you.

We use the infinitive (to + verb)

ContextExamples
to express purpose (= in order to)I went to the shop to buy bread.
after adjectives (happy, easy, difficult, important, glad, afraid, ready)It's easy to use. · I'm glad to help.
after certain verbs: want, would like, would love, need, decide, hope, plan, promise, offer, refuse, agree, manage, learn, expect, afford, seem, forget, choose, pretend, arrange, deserveI want to study medicine. · She decided to apply for the job. · We can't afford to travel.
after verb + object: want, ask, tell, advise, allow, encourage, expect, remind, teach, persuade + sb + toMy parents want me to study. · The teacher told us to be quiet.

Bare infinitive (no to) after modal verbs, after let, make + object and after had better: You must go. · They let me stay. · She made him apologise. · You'd better hurry.

Both forms

VerbMeaning
begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, preferno real change of meaning: It started raining / to rain.
remember / forget+ -ing = memory of a past action · + to = a duty: I remember locking the door. / Remember to lock the door.
stop+ -ing = quit · + to = in order to: He stopped smoking. / He stopped to smoke.
try+ -ing = experiment · + to = make an effort: Try turning it off. / I tried to open it.
Typical mistakes: I enjoy to read → I enjoy reading · I want going → I want to go · I'm interested to learn → I'm interested in learning · She made me to cry → She made me cry.

sebenta.title: Linking words
sebenta.html:
FunctionLinking wordsExamples
Contrastbut, yet (between clauses)
although / though / even though + clause
despite / in spite of + noun / -ing / the fact that
however / nevertheless / on the other hand (start of sentence, + comma)
whereas / while (comparison of two facts)		 It was cold, but we went out.
Although it was cold, we went out.
Despite the cold, we went out. · In spite of being tired, …
It was cold. However, we went out.
Some people recycle, whereas others don't care.
Cause / reasonbecause / as / since + clause
because of / due to / owing to + noun / -ing		 We stayed in because it was raining.
Flights were cancelled because of the storm.
Since you're here, you can help.
Consequence / resultso (between clauses)
therefore / consequently / as a result / that is why (+ comma)
so + adj + that; such (a) + noun + that		 It rained, so the match was cancelled.
It rained. As a result, the match was cancelled.
It was so hot that we stayed in. · It was such a hot day that…
Purposeto / in order to / so as to + infinitive
in order not to / so as not to + infinitive
so that + subject + can / will (present) · could / would (past)
for + noun / -ing		 I went out to buy bread.
I left early so as not to miss the bus.
I'll write it down so that I won't forget.
She saved money so that she could travel.
Additionand, also, too, as well, both … and, not only … but also
moreover / furthermore / in addition / besides / what is more		 He's clever and hard-working.
The hotel was cheap. Moreover, it was central.
Sequence / timefirst(ly), secondly, then, next, after that, meanwhile, finally; when, while, as soon as, until, by the time First, boil the water. Then add the pasta. Finally, …
Examplefor example / for instance / such as / likeRenewable energy, such as solar and wind power.
Opinion / conclusionin my opinion / in my view / personally / I believe
in conclusion / to sum up / all in all / on the whole		In my opinion, uniforms are a good idea.
To sum up, we must act now.
Although + subject + verb (although it was raining) ≠ despite / in spite of + noun / -ing (despite the rain · despite being tired). Despite of · Although of. However starts a new sentence and takes a comma; but joins two clauses in the same sentence.
Opinion essay plan: ① Introduction (present the topic + your opinion) ② First argument (Firstly… For instance…) ③ Second argument (Moreover… As a result…) ④ Opposite view (Some people argue that… However…) ⑤ Conclusion (To sum up… In my opinion…). One paragraph per idea; 120–150 words.

sebenta.title: Phrasal verbs
sebenta.html:
A phrasal verb = verb + particle (adverb and/or preposition) with a new meaning: give up = stop, look after = take care of. They are very common in spoken and informal English; in formal writing, a one-word verb is often preferred (find out → discover, put off → postpone).

Separable or inseparable?

TypeRuleExamples
Separable (with an object)the object can go after the particle or between verb and particle; a pronoun must go betweenTurn off the light. / Turn the light off.
Turn it off. (not turn off it)
Inseparablethe object always goes after the particleShe looks after her brother. / She looks after him.
Without objectno object at allThe plane took off. · Prices went up.
Three-partverb + adverb + preposition; inseparableI can't put up with the noise. · We've run out of time.

Particles and their typical meanings

  • up = completely / increase: eat up, use up, speed up, turn up · down = decrease / to the ground: slow down, turn down, cut down, write down
  • on = continue: go on, carry on, keep on · off = away / disconnected: take off, set off, turn off, put off
Phrasal verbs change tense like normal verbs: She gave up sugar. · They have set up a charity. · He is looking for a job. After look forward to, give up, keep on use -ing: I look forward to hearing from you.

sebenta.title: Modal verbs: overview
sebenta.html:
Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive, have no -s in the 3rd person and form negatives and questions without do: She must go. · Can he swim? · You needn't worry. Semi-modals: have to, need to, be able to, ought to, be allowed to, had better.

FunctionModalsExamples
Abilitycan / can't (present), could / couldn't (past), be able to (other tenses)I can speak French. · I could swim at five.
You'll be able to walk in a week.
Permissioncan (informal), may (formal), could (polite), be allowed toCan I use your phone? · May I come in?
We're allowed to use dictionaries.
Requestscan / could / will / would you…?Could you open the window, please?
Obligationmust (speaker's authority), have to (external rule), need to; past: had toI must finish this today. · I have to wear a uniform.
We had to wait for an hour.
No obligationdon't have to, don't need to, needn'tYou don't have to come if you're busy.
Prohibitionmustn't, can't, not be allowed toYou mustn't use your phone in class.
Adviceshould / shouldn't, ought to, had better (not)You should see a doctor. · You'd better not be late.
Possibilitymay / might / could + verbIt might rain later. · She may be at home.
Deduction (sure)must + verb (sure it is true)
can't + verb (sure it is not true)		The lights are on – they must be at home.
That can't be Ana – she's in Paris.
Offers / suggestionsshall I / we…?, would you like…?, could, why don't we…?Shall I help you? · We could go by bus.
mustn't = it is forbidden (You mustn't smoke here.) ≠ don't have to = it isn't necessary (You don't have to pay.). must (I decide) vs have to (a rule decides): I must study more. / I have to be at school at 8.

Modals in the past

PresentPastExample
can (ability)could / was able toI could read at four.
must / have tohad toI had to work last Saturday.
mustn't / can't (prohibition)wasn't / weren't allowed toWe weren't allowed to go out.
don't have todidn't have toWe didn't have to pay.
should (advice)should have + past participle (regret / criticism)I should have listened to you.
must / may / can't (deduction)must / may / can't have + past participleThe ground is wet – it must have rained.
Modals in the passive: modal + be + past participle: Plastic should be recycled. · The problem can't be solved overnight. · Rules must be followed. Modals in reported speech: can → could, will → would, may → might, must → had to: "I can help." → He said he could help.
